operator_plays.name: 24-to-72-Hour Escrow-Locked Transactional ("Flash") Double-Close Funding
operator_plays.mechanism: Fund the A->B acquisition only after the title agent independently verifies cleared, unconditional end-buyer B->C funds in escrow and an enforceable closing waterfall. Target a 1.0%–2.5% earned funding fee per 1–3 day turn; closing delays, fraud and legal restrictions can impair returns or principal.
inputs: Executed A->B and B->C purchase contracts, title commitment and independently verified settlement-agent credentials
Cleared end-buyer escrow funds, written disbursement conditions and a reconciled same-transaction payoff waterfall
Commercial-purpose funding agreement reviewed for applicable licensing, usury and escrow requirements
workflow: 1. Underwrite both contracts, title exceptions, end-buyer closing conditions and the settlement agent's authority and applicable bonding or insurance.
2. Independently confirm end-buyer cleared funds and irrevocable disbursement instructions using a previously verified title-agent contact channel.
3. Wire A->B funding only to approved title escrow after all release conditions are satisfied and the closing sequence is documented.
4. Reconcile B->C settlement, recover principal and earned fees, and release capital for reuse only after cleared repayment is confirmed.
metrics: Earned funding fees as a percentage of funded principal per completed turn
Median and maximum hours from funding disbursement to cleared repayment
Unrecovered principal and delayed-closing exposure as a percentage of outstanding funding

platform_risks.failure_mode: Fraudulent wire instructions or conditional end-buyer funds leave the A->B advance unrepaid
platform_risks.trigger: Last-minute beneficiary changes, failed independent callbacks or unresolved B->C release conditions
platform_risks.impact: Loss of principal, prolonged escrow disputes and interruption of capital recycling
platform_risks.detection_metric: Count of unresolved wire-verification exceptions and funded closings past contractual repayment deadlines
platform_risks.fallback: Stop disbursement, independently reverify settlement instructions and obtain counsel-directed escrow recovery before further funding

operator_plays.name: Earnest-Money Deposit ("Gator") Escrow Lending & Joint-Venture Splits
operator_plays.mechanism: Advance $2,500–$25,000 refundable-contingency earnest-money deposits directly to title escrow under documented JV or promissory protections, with security recorded or perfected where legally appropriate. Negotiate a 15%–30% share of an earned assignment fee or a lawful fixed return; refunds depend on contractual deadlines, valid contingency exercise and escrow release terms.
inputs: Assignable purchase agreement with explicit refundable contingencies, notice procedures and deadline calendar
Verified title escrow account and executed JV or promissory documents with legally appropriate recorded or perfected protections
Borrower diligence, assignment economics and state-specific lending, brokerage, securities and usury review
workflow: 1. Verify assignment rights, counterparty identity, refundable contingencies and the enforceability of the proposed JV or lending structure.
2. Execute repayment and profit-split documents, perfect any lawful security and transmit the deposit directly to verified title escrow.
3. Track contingency and assignment deadlines, require documented progress and deliver timely cancellation notices when authorized and necessary.
4. Reconcile the closing or refund statement, recover deposited principal and collect only the contractually earned fee or lawful return.
metrics: Earned assignment-fee share or fixed return per completed deposit advance
Percentage of active deposits with verified unexpired refund rights and complete documentation
Deposit loss rate and median days from advance to cleared repayment

platform_risks.failure_mode: A supposedly refundable deposit becomes nonrefundable or disputed
platform_risks.trigger: Missed contingency notice deadline, invalid cancellation or unauthorized contract amendment
platform_risks.impact: Deposit forfeiture, delayed recovery and disputes over assignment proceeds
platform_risks.detection_metric: Deposits approaching contingency expiry without documented assignment or cancellation instructions
platform_risks.fallback: Freeze additional advances, seek timely authorized cancellation and pursue counsel-reviewed escrow release or contractual remedies

operator_plays.name: Aged Shelf-Corp Reinstatement, Primary Tradeline & 0%-APR Corporate Credit Stacking
operator_plays.mechanism: Compare reinstated entities and genuine business credit facilities for working-capital financing; entity age is not operating history, and promotional APR economics require accurate underwriting and repayment capacity.
inputs: Entity filings, beneficial ownership, and liability searches
Verified operating financials and genuine supplier tradelines
Lender eligibility, promotional APR, fee, and guarantee terms
workflow: 1. Audit the entity's ownership, tax liabilities, and reinstatement requirements
2. Disclose acquisition and actual operating history; establish only genuine paid supplier accounts
3. Compare lender-approved applications with full debt disclosure and consolidated exposure limits
4. Fund documented business expenses and repay before promotional expiry using cash-flow reserves
metrics: Effective borrowing cost including fees
Debt service coverage under post-promotion APR
Utilization and days to promotional expiry

platform_risks.trigger: Misstated operating history, undisclosed debt, or expired promotional terms
platform_risks.impact: Account closure, accelerated repayment, and guarantee exposure
platform_risks.detection_metric: Underwriting discrepancies and stressed repayment coverage
platform_risks.fallback: Halt applications, correct disclosures, and use a transparent term facility or reduce financed spending

operator_plays.name: B2B Commercial Virtual Card (VCC) Interchange & AP Settlement Rebate Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Embedding a 'Free Automated Accounts Payable (AP) / Instant Vendor Settlement' platform inside high-volume B2B verticals (freight brokerage, construction general contracting, medical supply, property management, media agencies) that converts checks and ACH payables into single-use Visa/Mastercard Commercial Virtual Credit Cards (VCCs)—capturing 140–195 basis points (1.40%–1.95%) in uncapped commercial interchange rebates on hundreds of millions in third-party invoice volume.
inputs: BaaS / Commercial Card Issuing bank partnership (Marqeta, Lithic, Stripe Issuing, Highnote, Cross River) on uncapped Visa/Mastercard Large-Ticket & Purchasing interchange tiers
ERP/accounting connector (QuickBooks, NetSuite, Sage, McLeod/TMW freight TMS) ingesting open vendor AP ledgers
Automated vendor-enablement call/email engine pitching 'Day-1 Instant Payment via Virtual Card vs. Net-45 Check/ACH'
workflow: Onboard mid-market companies with $20M–$250M/yr in fragmented vendor payables onto a $0-cost AP automation and working-capital portal
Cross-reference their vendor master list against Visa/Mastercard supplier-acceptance networks to flag vendors that already accept card payments
Offer remaining vendors immediate Day-1 invoice settlement via single-use emailed/API virtual card in exchange for waiving Net-30/Net-60 wait times
Earn 1.50%–1.95% gross interchange rebate from the issuing bank on every settled dollar, sharing 0.25%–0.50% with the corporate client while retaining 1.10%–1.45% net platform margin
metrics: Total annualized Gross Payment Volume (GPV $) converted from ACH/check to Virtual Card (target: 25–45% of total AP)
Net retained interchange spread in basis points (110–145 bps) after bank processor fees and client revenue share
Vendor card-acceptance retention rate (%) across repeat monthly invoices

platform_risks.failure_mode: Vendor card-surcharging pushback or Visa/Mastercard Level-2/Level-3 large-ticket interchange downgrade
platform_risks.trigger: Large vendors refusing card settlement or failing to pass Level-3 line-item tax/invoice metadata with the authorization
platform_risks.impact: Shift of specific vendors back to low-margin ACH or interchange rate step-down
platform_risks.detection_metric: Automated Level-2/Level-3 data-enrichment pass rate and per-vendor surcharge detection
platform_risks.fallback: Automatically inject Level-3 line-item invoice metadata at card creation, offer dynamic early-pay ACH discounts (1.5%–2% 10-day net) for card-averse vendors, and focus on fragmented long-tail vendor bases

operator_plays.name: Whitelisted Agency Ad-Spend Card-Multiplier Points & Volume-Rebate Cycling
operator_plays.mechanism: Route genuine client-authorized advertising spend through eligible agency payment arrangements to earn contract-permitted rewards and volume rebates, net of financing, processing, and client pass-through obligations.

Issuer reward categories, caps, and repayment terms
Platform invoices and agency volume-rebate agreements
workflow: 1. Verify client authorization, platform payment permissions, and ownership of rewards and rebates
2. Model eligible media purchases against reward caps, fees, liquidity, and rebate thresholds

operator_plays.name: UCC-1 Filing, MCA Stacking & Maturity-Date Trigger Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Monitor state Secretary of State UCC-1 financing statements and continuation filings to identify operating businesses 4–9 months into high-cost Merchant Cash Advances (MCAs) or equipment notes, triggering refinance and debt-consolidation live transfers.

Secured-party lender dictionary (identifying MCA vs. bank/SBA filings)
Live-transfer commercial refinance & SBA consolidation desk
workflow: Classify daily UCC-1 filings by secured party to isolate businesses that took high-cost short-term working capital 120–240 days ago
Enrich business owner direct phone and email and score by industry revenue stability
Contact merchants during peak renewal/payoff windows to offer lower-rate term consolidation or equipment refinancing, monetizing via broker points or live-transfer fees

Live-transfer qualification rate (%)
Origination commission / referral fee per funded refi

platform_risks.detection_metric: 100% DNC/litigator-scrub pass rate and statutory APR disclosure audit in regulated states

operator_plays.name: MCA UCC-1 Trigger Stacking & Dual-Sided Default-Restructure Brokerage
operator_plays.mechanism: Use UCC filing changes to identify businesses that may need cash-flow review and consensual MCA restructuring, with verified obligations and disclosed compensation rather than encouraging undisclosed stacking.
inputs: Public UCC filings and termination records
Merchant-authorized contracts and cash-flow statements
Broker licensing rules and disclosed creditor compensation terms
workflow: 1. Treat UCC changes as outreach signals, not proof of default, and obtain merchant authorization
2. Reconcile advances, liens, repayment pulls, covenants, and sustainable payment capacity
3. Disclose dual-sided fees and conflicts; use independent counsel where representation would conflict
4. Coordinate documented creditor-approved modifications and monitor actual payment relief

Creditor-approved modification rate

chapters.question_prompt: How does a double closing actually work step by step, and how do wholesalers run back-to-back A-B and B-C closings with little or no money of their own?
chapters.title: The Double Close Playbook
chapters.subtitle: Back-to-back, simultaneous, and same-day double closings; A-B/B-C and ABC closings; triple closings; flash cash; double-escrow contracts; REO simultaneous closings; the end buyer funding both sides; and real no-money deal walkthroughs
chapters.executive_summary: Wholesalers, title operators and transactional lenders converge on one structure: two contracts, two independent back-to-back closings, so the seller never sees the resale price and the end buyer never sees the buy price. They reach for it when a spread crosses roughly $10,000 to $20,000, when REO, HUD, hedge-fund or no-assignment paper blocks assignments, and as states and title underwriters shut down pass-through funding and blind HUDs. Funders price at 1% to 3% of purchase, flat $850 to $2,000, or 1% plus $100, wire only after the end buyer's cash sits in escrow, and get repaid on the B-to-C leg, often within an hour. The split: Kevin Tacher and the funders insist leg one closes with outside cash, while Jerry Norton, Luigi Ontiveros, Travis Stagg and Rick use the end buyer's wire to fund both legs.

key_metrics.label: Transactional Funding Fee Range
key_metrics.value: 1% to 3% of the purchase price, plus the wholesaler's closing costs
key_metrics.context: Ricky's quoted rate at Flip Lab Capital for same-day double closes where the end buyer's cash is already with title

key_metrics.label: Bright Closings Pricing Above $75,000
key_metrics.value: 1% of purchase price plus $100 processing; flat $850 below $75,000
key_metrics.context: A $100,000 purchase costs $1,100, paid out of the second closing with nothing out of pocket

key_metrics.label: Velocity Capital Upfront Initiation Fee
key_metrics.value: $250, subtracted from the back-end fee when the deal closes
key_metrics.context: Pete Russell added the fee to filter out wholesalers who submit deals and then back out, keeping pricing low under volume

key_metrics.label: Minimum Non-Refundable Buyer Deposit
key_metrics.value: $2,500 minimum; $5,000 up to $10,000 preferred
key_metrics.context: Jerry Norton's requirement at contract execution so the cash buyer does not flake on the day of closing

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner here defines the double close the same way: two separate contracts, two separate closings, same property, run back-to-back. Kevin Tacher of Independence Title says the art is making closing A and closing B close independently, so a title claim on one never touches the other, and the shop records deed one by e-recording, typically same day or next, before following with deed two [lLbfcHAX30o @ 00:01:09]. Ryan Schrope, who has run over 135 lending transactions in a year, draws the hard line: an A-to-B contract plus a B-to-C contract closing on the same day, and if only one contract exists, it is just an assignment, not a double close [j30R1Cef6PE @ 00:07:19]. Pete Russell of Velocity Capital frames the flow in plain numbers: seller contract at $100,000, separate end-buyer contract at $150,000, the funder wires the full $100,000 to the attorney or title company, the first closing records, the second closing settles, and the closing company disburses profit to the wholesaler and principal plus fee to the funder [qtTEzFSMqJg @ 00:05:21]. Because the seller only signs closing one and the end buyer only signs closing two, usually remotely and at separate times, neither side ever sees the other's number, which is the entire point of running the structure.

The consensus driver is protecting the spread. Russell has had deals die at the table: an attorney and seller went line by line through a HUD, saw the wholesaler's business name next to $30,000, decided it was unearned and walked out, while savvy buyers who spot a big assignment fee come back weeks later claiming mold in the crawl space and demanding $10,000 to $15,000 off [qtTEzFSMqJg @ 00:09:34]. Ricky of Flip Lab puts the tolerance line near $20,000: above that, plenty of sellers and buyers start 'looking in your pockets,' so on a big spread paying $5,000 to $7,000 to double close is worth it because less can go wrong [Qk7hhsytc9Y @ 00:04:42]. Jerry Norton of Flipping Mastery TV sets the comfort zone lower, saying most cash buyers shrug at fees under $10,000 or $15,000 but balk at $20,000, $25,000, $30,000 or higher, and adds the forced case: bank REOs and short sales carry no-assignment clauses, so the double close becomes mandatory [Jfl-5LgDTaM @ 00:04:32]. Dave Dinkle of LearnREInvesting has watched sellers refuse to close over an investor profit of only $2,500, so 'too large' sits squarely in the eye of the beholder [_QXnSUQsTNw @ 00:02:41].

The baseline prerequisites repeat across every channel. First, a closing company that genuinely handles double closes: Norton warns the wrong title company will kill the deal, so he hard-codes the investor-friendly closer into both the seller and buyer contracts [Jfl-5LgDTaM @ 00:09:40], and Schrope asks 'do you understand the double close' on the very first call, because some title shops have never done one and some refuse outright [j30R1Cef6PE @ 00:12:42]. Second, an end buyer whose cash is actually sitting in escrow before anyone wires leg one, a condition every funder in this group treats as non-negotiable. Third, regulation is herding wholesalers into this structure. Russell reports Tennessee closers shutting down pass-through funding and blind HUDs, yet says not one attorney, escrow or title company nationwide has told clients no on a straight double close, and David Olds, whose company owns a title operation in six states, notes closers like it because they book two sets of fees, roughly an extra $300 [KG3yn1b1Yr4 @ 00:07:54]. Dinkle sees the same shift from the funding side: as more states ban assignments, sales of contracts and joint venture agreements, investors are adopting double closings as standard operating procedure rather than a last resort [_QXnSUQsTNw @ 00:03:58].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On the capital side, transactional funding, which Tacher also calls flash funding, covers the A-to-B purchase as an unsecured loan with no mortgage or note signed, repaid as an unsecured payoff on the B-to-C closing, and the closer issues title insurance on both legs [lLbfcHAX30o @ 00:02:17]. Pricing varies by shop. Ricky's Flip Lab Capital charges one to three percent of the purchase price, and Ricky runs the math openly: a $200,000 buy at 2% is $4,000, plus about $3,000 in closing costs, so $7,000 in fees comes off what would have been a $20,000 assignment [Qk7hhsytc9Y @ 00:02:49]. Jasper Cool's Bright Closings charges 1% of the purchase price plus a $100 processing fee above $75,000, so $1,100 on a $100,000 house, and a flat $850 below $75,000, all paid from the second closing; the shop funds every state except New York, Alaska and Hawaii, answers submissions within 5 to 10 minutes and can fund the same morning [EUE6UWl2qBA @ 00:03:19]. Russell's Velocity Capital prices off the amount funded, asks for no 10% to 20% down, and collects nothing upfront except a $250 initiation fee credited back at closing, a fee added only because heavy volume brought too many deals that were submitted and then abandoned [qtTEzFSMqJg @ 00:14:38].

Underwriting is the deal, not the borrower. Russell says Velocity ignores credit score, experience and profit size; if the deal reaches the closing line and everything lines up, it funds, and more than 50% of monthly clients are repeat users who switched every deal over after the first one [KG3yn1b1Yr4 @ 00:13:29]. Intake is a short form: Bright Closings asks for the borrower name exactly as it appears on the seller contract, phone, email, property address, A-to-B purchase price, closing date, the closing attorney or title company with contact details, whether that closer already knows it is a double close, and uploads of both signed contracts [EUE6UWl2qBA @ 00:00:49]. Schrope's lending workflow then runs entirely through the title officer: confirm the A-to-B HUD to learn the true wire amount, send a payoff letter on letterhead committing title to hold the money in escrow and return principal plus fee, approve the B-to-C HUD showing the lender's LLC payoff, and wait for the end buyer's funds [j30R1Cef6PE @ 00:15:20]. Every funder here wires last. Ricky funds only after title confirms the end buyer's cash is on hand, which leaves the lender exposed mainly to bad wires, disputes or a bad title company, and Flip Lab passes on hedge-fund deals needing 30-day gaps between closings [Qk7hhsytc9Y @ 00:06:50].

The wholesaler-side mechanics center on paper, timing and earnest money. Norton's closing-in-escrow run sheet on a $220,000 buy and $250,000 resale: seller signs at 10 a.m., the wholesaler signs both sides at 11 a.m. bringing no money, the cash buyer signs and wires $250,000 at 1 p.m., the wire lands at 2 p.m., title pays $220,000 to the seller and $30,000 to the wholesaler, then records closing one before closing two, leaving the wholesaler around $300 to $500 in fees [Jfl-5LgDTaM @ 00:08:20]. Norton's buyer contracts demand at least $2,500 non-refundable, preferably $5,000 to $10,000, plus a clause instructing escrow to release the deposit as damages with no further instruction needed. Luigi Ontiveros's double-escrow resale contract closes in seven to ten days, requires $10,000 non-refundable by 2 p.m. the next day, and charges the buyer $200 per day once funding slips past 48 hours after escrow requests funds [UpxkrBIxTtQ @ 00:06:05]. Russell keeps the seller-side deposit near $500 in attorney escrow behind an inspection period and clear-title contingency, wants $3,000 to $5,000 going hard from the end buyer, and reuses the same one-page seller contract with roles flipped for the B-to-C side [qtTEzFSMqJg @ 00:18:00].

callout.title: How the operators squeeze cost and friction out of the double close
callout.body: Small moves the practitioners use to keep fees down and keep both legs closing on schedule.
items: Keep B-to-C closing costs on the end buyer as if it were an assignment, then ask the title company for a break on A-to-B costs since they earn double in about an hour [Closer Control — qtTEzFSMqJg @ 00:13:04]

sop_steps.title: Lock both contracts
sop_steps.action: Sign the A-to-B seller contract and a separate B-to-C contract with the end buyer before requesting funds.
sop_steps.detail: Funders will not spend time until both signed contracts exist; with only one contract it is an assignment, not a double close [Ryan Schrope — j30R1Cef6PE @ 00:09:00]

sop_steps.title: Submit the deal and introduce the closer
sop_steps.action: Submit contact info, address, amount needed and closing date, then introduce the funder to the title company or attorney.
sop_steps.detail: Velocity's team then works directly with the closing professional on delays and final amounts instead of chasing the wholesaler [David Olds REI — KG3yn1b1Yr4 @ 00:11:44]

sop_steps.title: Paper the payoff
sop_steps.action: Confirm the A-to-B HUD amount, deliver a payoff letter, and approve a B-to-C HUD showing the funder's payoff.
sop_steps.detail: Title signs a letterhead payoff agreeing to hold funds in escrow and return principal plus fee; expect corrections because title rarely gets the HUD right on the first try [Ryan Schrope — j30R1Cef6PE @ 00:16:22]

sop_steps.title: Fund last, then disburse
sop_steps.action: Wire leg-one money only after all docs are signed and the end buyer's funds sit in escrow.
sop_steps.detail: Velocity is the last piece of the puzzle, wiring once closing docs are signed and the end buyer has fully committed money into escrow [David Olds REI — KG3yn1b1Yr4 @ 00:12:46]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in the double-close game is whose money hits closing A. Kevin Tacher of Independence Title draws a hard line: both legs close independently, the end buyer's money never funds the first closing, and closing A must close cash, so their shop arranges transactional or flash funding as an unsecured loan with no mortgage or note, repaid as an unsecured payoff on closing B [lLbfcHAX30o @ 00:02:01]. Jerry Norton of Flipping Mastery TV runs the opposite play: every party signs in escrow, the end cash buyer wires $250,000, and title uses that wire to fund closing one, paying the seller $220,000 and the wholesaler $30,000 before recording both deeds in order, with the wholesaler hiding the fee and skipping transactional funding costs entirely [Jfl-5LgDTaM @ 00:08:37]. Travis Stagg of Forefront Enterprises runs the same mechanic on a $20,000 buy and $25,000 resale: title pays the seller out of the buyer's funds and sends the $5,000 difference, so the only skin in the game is a $500 to $2,000 deposit, letting an operator run ten or twenty times as many deals [Qe97wvpylvo @ 00:01:29]. William Bronchick calls it pure sequencing: deeds and funds sit in escrow, either side can sign first, and nothing records until every piece is complete [Z9NzpNmbuu8 @ 00:02:39].

Whether end-buyer money can still touch the A leg depends on who holds the pen. Pete Russell of Velocity Capital reports wholesalers calling because blind HUDs and pass-through funding are being phased out, and host David Olds, who owns a title company in six states, says underwriters like First American, Old Republic, WFG and Fidelity see pass-through as something that just looks like fraud [KG3yn1b1Yr4 @ 00:07:27]. Jason Gaston calls the end-buyer-funded simultaneous closing frowned upon though still done in many places, and routes around it with transactional funders charging a flat one to two thousand dollars [JbOkaP42JKo @ 00:01:47]. Dave Dinkle of LearnREInvesting says most closing agents and title insurers refuse these transactions, and the disclosure needed to make them work is usually a deal-killer because seller and end buyer then see the profit [_QXnSUQsTNw @ 00:03:26]. Rick of Flip With Rick refuses to concede the point: have the title company prepare a directive the cash buyer signs, authorizing part of a $150,000 purchase to fund the $110,000 A leg with the $40,000 balance going to the wholesaler, or accept a blind or split HUD when a friendly title company offers one, which Rick says most will not [4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:10:54].

Operators also split on when a spread justifies paying for two closings. Luigi Ontiveros draws a hard line at $10,000: anything above it, even $11,000, goes through a double escrow that costs only three to five hundred dollars extra, because buyers who see big profits kill deals [UpxkrBIxTtQ @ 00:01:10]. Ricky of Flip Lab sets the pain point higher, saying many buyers and sellers start looking in your pockets once an assignment fee passes roughly $20,000, and that on big spreads paying five or seven thousand dollars to double close buys security and less that can go wrong [Qk7hhsytc9Y @ 00:04:42]. Rick flips the logic on buyers entirely: never switch to a double close because a cash buyer resents the fee, drop that buyer and find another, and save the double close for sellers spooked by a realtor sister, lawyer or other outside party [4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:13:39]. Pete Russell takes the opposite stance, telling wholesalers clearing $20,000 to $50,000 that an extra couple thousand in A-to-B costs is cost of business next to a buyer demanding a $5,000 to $10,000 reduction or a seller walking out at the table, and recommends asking the title company for a break since it earns double fees in about an hour [qtTEzFSMqJg @ 00:14:04].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failures start with a visible spread. Pete Russell had a seller and their attorney go line by line through a HUD, spot the business name beside $30,000, decide the fee was unearned and walk away from the closing table, even though the seller had been prepped that the contract would go to a partner at the agreed price [qtTEzFSMqJg @ 00:09:34]. Russell has also been stung by savvy buyers who spot a large assignment fee weeks before closing, then return claiming mold in the crawl space and demanding $10,000 to $15,000 off, so even a negotiated $5,000 cut comes straight out of the wholesaler's pocket [qtTEzFSMqJg @ 00:10:18]. Rick warns that a realtor relative can show up at closing vowing to bust the assignment fee, and that lawyers, title companies or the seller can blow a deal up the same way, especially when the wholesaler hid the profit instead of telling the seller up front that they are an investor out to make money [4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:03:52]. David Olds sees the same pattern nationally: title companies tightening policy, states regulating assignment fees and buyers reading deal structure, so transparency on big fees kills deals that once closed easily [KG3yn1b1Yr4 @ 00:00:21].

The second trap is the closer itself. Jerry Norton says flatly that the wrong title company will kill your deal, so the investor-friendly closer should be named in both the seller and buyer contracts with a clause binding each side to use that company [Jfl-5LgDTaM @ 00:09:40]. Dave Dinkle watched a closing agent tell a new investor that the attorney-owned firm could not legally do an ABC closing, because the term meant something different to that agent; moving the file to a high-volume investor closer worked, but the two-day deadline had to be extended [_QXnSUQsTNw @ 00:02:09]. Ryan Schrope, with over 135 lending transactions in a year, screens title on whether they wire at all, since a check-only shop can lock up $100,000 for five to seven days plus deposit holds, and reports title rarely gets the B-to-C HUD payoff right on the first try [j30R1Cef6PE @ 00:11:46]. Pete Russell fields panicked calls from wholesalers whose title company announced at the last minute that the old pass-through method was dead, asking for funding tomorrow or in two days, and needs extra lead time on double closings over a million [KG3yn1b1Yr4 @ 00:09:27].

Then run the math before celebrating any spread. Ricky of Flip Lab prices a $200,000 purchase against a $220,000 resale: a 2% transactional fee of $4,000 plus about $3,000 in closing costs strips $7,000 out of a $20,000 spread, money the wholesaler simply keeps on a straight assignment [Qk7hhsytc9Y @ 00:02:49]. Rick says a $10,000 double close can net as little as four grand once $5,000 to $6,000 in closing costs hit the HUD, and that taking title means owning a house you never planned to own if the cash buyer fails, plus a whirlwind of IRS paperwork from stacked HUDs [4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:05:40]. Jerry Norton learned the deposit lesson the hard way when a cash buyer flaked on closing day and refused to let escrow release a $5,000 non-refundable deposit, a big fight that produced a release clause letting escrow pay the wholesaler without further instruction [Jfl-5LgDTaM @ 00:12:19]. Pete Russell got burned from the other side, posting non-refundable money with sellers who took it and ran, and now parks about $500 in escrow behind an inspection period and clear-title contingency [qtTEzFSMqJg @ 00:18:44].

callout.title: Four Checks Before Any Double Close Goes To The Table
callout.body: Every gate below traces to a deal that stalled, blew up, or bled money for a named operator. Clear all four before committing the A-to-B leg.
items: No money moves on the A leg until the end buyer's B-to-C funds are sitting in escrow, because promised same-day funding is worth nothing until it lands [Ryan Schrope — j30R1Cef6PE @ 00:18:13].

Tell the closing agent exactly which structure you want before sending contracts, and ask your transactional funder first if unsure, since an ABC closing means different things to different agents [LearnREInvesting — _QXnSUQsTNw @ 00:04:14].

Lock the cash buyer with a minimum $2,500 non-refundable deposit, preferably $5,000 to $10,000, backed by a release clause that needs no further escrow instruction [Flipping Mastery TV — Jfl-5LgDTaM @ 00:11:27].

Screen bank-owned and short sale deals for deed restrictions barring resale for 30, 60 or 90 days or above a set percentage before promising a double close [Game Changer Real Estate Insights — lLbfcHAX30o @ 00:03:38].

chapters.pull_quote: "Don't ever do a double closing because you're scared of your cash buyer, you're not doing this business right." — Flip With Rick (4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:11:45).
action_checklist: Run the spread test on every contract: assign deals at or under $10,000 and push anything above it, even $11,000, into a double escrow [Luigi Ontiveros — UpxkrBIxTtQ @ 00:01:10].
Write a clause into both the seller and buyer contracts naming your investor-friendly title, escrow or attorney company as the agreed closer [Flipping Mastery TV — Jfl-5LgDTaM @ 00:09:55].
Build the right to assign to another entity you want to close with directly into every offer so assignment permission is never the bottleneck [Ron LeGrand — Rrp7i7rV1lo @ 00:01:05].

Reuse your own one-page seller contract for the B-to-C leg with you as seller, keep B-to-C closing costs on the end buyer, and ask title for a break on A-to-B costs [Closer Control — qtTEzFSMqJg @ 00:16:29].

Submit the signed A-to-B and B-to-C contracts, closing date and closing attorney contact to your transactional funder, and confirm the attorney already knows it is a double close [Jasper Cool — EUE6UWl2qBA @ 00:02:02].

Add a 48-hour funding requirement and a $200 per-day delay charge to the buyer contract so the end buyer cannot take their sweet time once escrow requests funds [Luigi Ontiveros — UpxkrBIxTtQ @ 00:06:05].

chapters.question_prompt: When should a wholesaler assign the contract, when should they double close, and where does transactional funding fit when neither option works?
chapters.title: Assign, Double Close, or Fund the Transaction
chapters.subtitle: Assignment vs. double close vs. double escrow; protecting the spread; state rules (including Michigan); when assignments and double closes aren't allowed; transactional funding basics for wholesalers and realtor-wholesalers; and closing when your cash is tied up
chapters.executive_summary: Wholesalers across these playbooks treat the assignment as the default cheap exit and the double close as the tool for three jobs: no-assignment contracts on bank, REO, HUD and auction inventory; hiding a fat spread from a squirmy seller or salty buyer; and showing up as buyer of record. Transactional funding bankrolls the A-to-B leg for minutes to a day, with no credit check, against a documented end buyer, typically costing 1-3% of the funded amount (quotes run from 0.5% to 4%, or $1,500-$5,000 flat). The switch point is the fight: Jamil Damji moved Key Glee's double-close trigger from $15,000 to $20,000, Brent Daniels and Lex Levinrad set it at $15,000 and $10,000, David Olds assigns up to $100,000, and Biz Matthew says assign no matter what.

key_metrics.label: Standard Transactional Funding Fee
key_metrics.value: 1% to 3% of the loan amount ($1,000 to $3,000 on a $100,000 loan)
key_metrics.context: Michael's typical lender pricing for same-day double-close funding, rising with term length and perceived deal risk.

key_metrics.label: Key Glee Double-Close Trigger
key_metrics.value: Profit above $20,000 (raised from $15,000)
key_metrics.context: Jamil Damji's house rule: assign anything at $20,000 or less, double close above it after finding sellers rarely objected.

key_metrics.label: Double-Close Profit Drag
key_metrics.value: $14,000 net vs. $20,000 on assignment (about $6,000-$7,000 lost to title)
key_metrics.context: David Olds' $100,000 contract resold at $120,000, run once as an assignment and once as a two-leg double close.

key_metrics.label: Purchase-Side Closing Cost Hit
key_metrics.value: $2,500 to $4,000 per double close, plus 1%-2% funding origination
key_metrics.context: Brent Daniels' estimate of closing costs the wholesaler eats on the A-to-B leg after promising the seller all fees are covered.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The default exit across this bench is the assignment. Lex Levinrad says the entire move is three words on the purchase contract, 'and or assigns,' after which you transfer your rights to a third party, skip the closing table, put up zero cash, and get wired your assignment fee by the title company while 'sitting on the beach somewhere' [ogZEBPqsJc4 @ 00:01:31]. Jerry Norton of Flipping Mastery TV calls the single-closing assignment the quickest and easiest way to wholesale because it needs no funding at all: the cash buyer funds the deal directly to the seller and you walk away with a big check [qWrqNQvtTO8 @ 00:00:52]. David Olds, who reports more than 1,500 wholesale deals out of Chattanooga, runs the clean version: contract at $100,000, sell the contract to an end buyer at $120,000, and the $20,000 difference is a check cut to you at closing by the title company [oXZTulq2Qx0 @ 00:00:55]. The shared weakness is visibility. Brent Daniels warns that the cash buyer sees your fee on the assignment agreement or the settlement statement, and buyers who decide you negotiated too well 'get a little bit chippy' and start throwing wrenches into the end of the transaction to make you take less [1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:07:06].

When the assignment breaks, the consensus fallback is the double close. Odardo LLC lays it out as A, B, and C: A sells to you in closing one, you sell to C in closing two, each leg carries its own contract, closing statement, and deed, and both usually run the same day, often back-to-back at the same title company [aHsBrb_hBYw @ 00:01:14]. Three triggers repeat. First, the contract is non-assignable: Jerry Norton says no-assignment clauses sit in all bank-owned inventory such as short sales and REOs, which forces a double close and transactional funding unless you know a workaround [qWrqNQvtTO8 @ 00:03:16]. Second, the spread is big enough to blow up the table. Jamil Damji says he has watched sellers walk out of the title company and refuse to sign closing documents after spotting a $10,000, $15,000, $20,000, and sometimes $50,000 assignment fee on a HUD [KMD0dZIIYwc @ 00:01:06]. Third, optics and credibility: Fuel My Deal lists being the actual buyer of record at the closing table as a reason on its own, next to assignments being barred by law, by the seller, or by the title company, and keeping the end buyer from seeing exactly what you make [y5I0Ma11ptA @ 00:00:41].

Transactional funding is the glue, and its definition barely moves from speaker to speaker. Michael of The Virtual Investor calls it a short-term loan repaid usually the same day and sometimes as long as a week, used almost exclusively for double closes, and says he and partner Paul have wholesaled REO properties in 44 states this way [kCbwtS3VKw4 @ 00:02:10]. Brett Flory sells it as no credit checks, no income requirements, and 100% financing of the purchase price, used to close deals where assignment isn't allowed while keeping the original purchase price private [QQEovor5ZiA @ 00:01:23]. Kemedia adds that the money typically comes from a hard money or private money lender and is only used when there is an established and well documented end buyer ready to buy immediately after the wholesaler purchases from the original seller [VXAZ4iN4Ha0 @ 00:00:36]. Sure Flow Capital Partners explains why you can't just use the buyer's check: the order of operations requires real money to fund the A-to-B purchase before the B-to-C leg funds to you, even though your buyer is paying you minutes later [sXh1jFRArig @ 00:01:40]. The payoff is identical across them: the lender is repaid out of the B-to-C proceeds, and the wholesaler keeps the spread minus fees and closing costs.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The fee is the whole unit-economics conversation, and the quotes spread wide. Fuel My Deal prices transactional funding at 1.5% to 3% of the funded amount or a flat fee, deducted at closing rather than paid upfront, so a $2,000 fee on a $15,000 spread walks you away with $13,000 [y5I0Ma11ptA @ 00:01:29]. Jerry Norton widens the band to 1% to 4%, or a flat $1,500 to $5,000, and stresses you pay the full fee even when the loan is retired five minutes later: fund $87,356 at 2% and you owe $1,747.12 [qWrqNQvtTO8 @ 00:02:09]. Gerald Harris quotes the low end at half a percent to 2%, or $500 to $2,000 on a $100,000 buy, pads his model to roughly $3,000 once transfer taxes land, and tells agent-investors to claw that back on the front end by buying at $97,000 instead of $100,000 [0Nli9p7r9jI @ 00:05:23]. Brent Daniels says a transactional lender typically charges a point or two for five or ten minutes of money, but once you build a reputation you can push the origination fee down to about $1,000, and he steers operators to local funders because the big national companies are tough to communicate with [1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:05:53].

Mechanically, the money lives inside escrow, not in your bank account. Dave Dinkle of LearnREInvesting insists that both the transactional funder's money and the end buyer's money land in the closing agent's escrow account by wire only, because counterfeit money orders and cashier's checks are easy to make on high-quality copiers [gCae6AF4TSo @ 00:00:52]. The lender, he says, only needs to review the closing statements for both legs, confirm the end buyer's funds have cleared and that there is a profit on the investor's side, then authorize the closing, which runs anywhere from 30 minutes to many hours; the funder's money is wired back usually the same day [gCae6AF4TSo @ 00:01:54]. Brent Daniels separates a double escrow, where the cash buyer's money funnels through you and funds your purchase, from a double close, where the title company wants you to wire in your own funds, which is exactly where transactional lenders step in for five minutes to typically no more than 24 or 48 hours [1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:04:53]. Longer holds cost real money: Michael of The Virtual Investor charges a flat fee or percentage plus 12% annualized if a deal slips past the one-to-three-day window, so a $150,000 loan runs $3,000 plus about $50 a day [kCbwtS3VKw4 @ 00:07:16].

The double close carries hard costs on top of the funding fee. David Olds walks a $100,000 contract up to $103,000 or $104,000 after closing costs and title insurance on the buy, adds another $1,000 to $2,000 on the resale, and lands at $14,000 profit instead of $20,000, with that missing money going to the title company for running two legs instead of one [oXZTulq2Qx0 @ 00:02:13]. Brent Daniels pegs the purchase-side hit at $2,500 to $4,000 because you promised the seller you would pay all closing costs, then stacks a 1% to 2% transactional origination fee on top [1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:09:48]. Jamil Damji explains why the math breaks in $700,000-to-$800,000 median markets like California, Austin, San Francisco, and Boston: seller's policies are tied to purchase price, so closing costs rise in direct proportion [KMD0dZIIYwc @ 00:04:37]. Jerry Norton flips the logic for whole-tailing: buy a structurally sound, $300,000-ARV cosmetic house at $200,000, sell it to a homeowner at $250,000 instead of wholesaling to an investor at $210,000, pay about $6,000 in time-based funding fees over 60 days to the kind of Phoenix lender charging 18% with no prepayment penalty, and still come out way ahead of a $10,000 single closing [qWrqNQvtTO8 @ 00:05:41].

callout.title: Street Moves That Cut Cost and Keep the Spread Intact
callout.body: Small structural choices the operators use to shave fees, find the right closer, and protect the buyer's exit.
items: Crowdsource your closer: post in local fix-and-flip or investor groups asking which escrow officers or closing attorneys actually do double escrows, since some do and some don't [Brent Daniels - Wholesaling Inc — 1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:03:10].

Hunt for title companies or attorneys that let the end buyer wire funds in the morning and use that money to close your A-to-B leg; a lot won't, but the ones that do let you skip the lender [Biz Matthew — ntGitnGf_xo @ 00:04:08].

Pre-pay the funding fee at the negotiating table: lock the seller at $97,000 instead of $100,000 so the transactional fee and transfer taxes come out of the discount, not your spread [Gerald Harris — 0Nli9p7r9jI @ 00:05:23].

Double close large spreads so the rehabber's purchase records at the real price; an assignment records at your contract price and retail lenders may under-appraise or kick back the flip [Jamil Damji — KMD0dZIIYwc @ 00:02:43].

sop_steps.title: Lock the contract and pick the exit
sop_steps.action: Check assignability and size the spread against your double-close trigger.
sop_steps.detail: If the seller is a bank, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, HUD, or an auction site, 'and or assigns' is off the table and you are double closing [Lex Levinrad Real Estate Training and Coaching — ogZEBPqsJc4 @ 00:02:44]; otherwise assign at $20,000 or less and double close above it, the Key Glee rule [Jamil Damji — KMD0dZIIYwc @ 00:02:28].

sop_steps.title: Paper the end buyer on a separate B-to-C contract
sop_steps.action: Sign a new purchase agreement with the end buyer at the higher price, set to close the same day.
sop_steps.detail: Strong funding files carry a clear purchase and sale agreement, a qualified end buyer, a profitable spread, and an investor-familiar title company [Sure Flow Capital Partners — AsVTF7HImUo @ 00:05:15]; without a buyer lined up, transactional lenders typically won't fund [The Virtual Investor — kCbwtS3VKw4 @ 00:02:27].

sop_steps.title: Submit to the funder and wire it into title
sop_steps.action: Send both contracts to the transactional lender and let them coordinate directly with title.
sop_steps.detail: Run the four-step plan: contract, submit the deal to the funder for review, coordinate with title, then close and collect [Sure Flow Capital Partners — AsVTF7HImUo @ 00:04:33]; the lender checks your purchase and sale agreement and sale agreement so both sides are complete before wiring [Jamil Damji — bnkxqdwWmdQ @ 00:00:38].

sop_steps.title: Close back-to-back and collect the spread
sop_steps.action: Sign both legs at the table with every dollar in escrow by wire, then take the difference.
sop_steps.detail: The funder's money closes the first leg, the end buyer's money funds the second within moments, and the funder is wired back usually the same day [LearnREInvesting — gCae6AF4TSo @ 00:02:23]; the fee comes out at closing, so a $2,000 fee on a $15,000 spread nets you $13,000 [Fuel My Deal — y5I0Ma11ptA @ 00:01:29].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is the fee threshold that flips an operator from assigning to double closing. Lex Levinrad runs the most conservative line: consider double closing once the assignment fee clears roughly $10,000. The Levinrad shop says it double closes almost all of its deals, partly because a $50,000 line on the HUD invites an end buyer to renegotiate down to $25,000 at the table [ogZEBPqsJc4 @ 00:02:14]. Jamil Damji's Key Glee team used to double close anything over $15,000 in profit. They moved the trigger to $20,000 after finding that sellers rarely say anything as long as they get what the purchase contract promised [KMD0dZIIYwc @ 00:02:12]. David Olds, citing more than 1,500 wholesale deals, sits at the opposite pole. Anything up to $100,000 goes out as an assignment, protected by a big enough deposit from the buyer. Olds reserves double closes for timing gaps or for fees so large the buyer should not see them [oXZTulq2Qx0 @ 00:03:22]. Biz Matthew goes further still, arguing that assignments are the way to go no matter what, even for large amounts. In that view, a buyer uncomfortable with a $40,000 to $50,000 fee is simply the wrong buyer for the business [ntGitnGf_xo @ 00:07:16].

Practitioners also disagree on whose nerves the double close is actually protecting. Biz Matthew frames it as a seller tool first. A paranoid seller who wants the wholesaler physically at the closing table, and who might kill the deal otherwise, is the best reason to buy and resell [ntGitnGf_xo @ 00:01:40]. Brent Daniels points the risk at the other side, warning that cash buyers who see the fee get chippy and salty and throw wrenches in late. The Daniels rule is to assign under $15,000 and to double escrow or double close above it. Operators then shift back toward assignments once repeat buyers stop counting their money [1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:12:25]. Jamil Damji adds a third beneficiary, the end buyer's exit. An assigned deal records at the contract price, so a rehabber who paid $200,000 on a $150,000 contract can face an under-appraisal or a refused loan from a retail lender. A double close records the price the buyer actually paid [KMD0dZIIYwc @ 00:03:30]. Gerald Harris argues from licensing rather than psychology. Harris tells licensed agents that straight assignments sit in a gray area under a higher ethical standard, and that closing and reselling with transactional funding is the cleaner break, including on the broker split [0Nli9p7r9jI @ 00:07:20].

The funding leg itself splits into competing playbooks. Brent Daniels separates two structures. In a double escrow, the cash buyer's money comes in and funds the wholesaler's purchase, so no money comes out of pocket. In a true double close, the title company demands that the wholesaler wire their own funds, and that is where transactional funding enters [1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:03:46]. Biz Matthew confirms that some title companies and attorneys will use a buyer's morning wire to close the A to B leg. A lot of them will not, which pushes operators back to a transactional lender [ntGitnGf_xo @ 00:04:26]. On hold length the speakers diverge hard. Michael of The Virtual Investor says that if no buyer is lined up, or a conventional-loan buyer is a month out, the right tool is a private or hard money lender rather than a transactional lender [kCbwtS3VKw4 @ 00:02:45]. Jerry Norton of Flipping Mastery TV instead stretches transactional money across a 30 to 90 day wholetail, naming a Phoenix lender at 18% interest with no prepayment penalty. Norton's example is a $200,000 buy resold at $250,000 to a homeowner, which still beats a $10,000 investor assignment after $6,000 in funding fees [qWrqNQvtTO8 @ 00:05:27]. Norton's math only works because the retail spread dwarfs the extra commissions and fees that cut into the wholesale profit.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most repeated firsthand failure is a deal dying at the table because somebody saw the spread. Jerry Norton of Flipping Mastery TV says flatly that a buyer and a seller have walked from a Norton closing because the wholesale fee was too high. According to Norton, fees of $25,000 to $30,000 make the seller feel underpaid and the buyer feel overcharged, even when both agreed to the numbers [qWrqNQvtTO8 @ 00:04:15]. Jamil Damji reports watching sellers walk out of the title company and refuse to sign closing documents. Each had spotted a $10,000, $15,000, $20,000 or even $50,000 assignment fee on the HUD. That is why a hard-negotiated, squirmy seller gets a double close by default [KMD0dZIIYwc @ 00:01:06]. Lex Levinrad describes the buyer-side version: a $50,000 assignment line raises eyebrows and invites a last-minute demand to cut the fee in half [ogZEBPqsJc4 @ 00:01:58]. Brent Daniels says cash buyers who resent a hard-negotiated price start throwing wrenches in at the end of the transaction. The goal is to make the wholesaler nervous enough to take less. Daniels also warns that drama at close burns time that should have gone into hunting the next opportunity [1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:07:23].

Double closing has a real price, and several operators run the math to show it. David Olds walks through a $100,000 contract resold at $120,000. Closing costs and title insurance push the basis to roughly $103,000 or $104,000, and the second leg adds another $1,000 or $2,000. The profit shrinks from $20,000 to about $14,000, with the missing $6,000 to $7,000 going to the title company for running two legs [oXZTulq2Qx0 @ 00:02:28]. Brent Daniels puts the purchase-side hit at $2,500 to $4,000 when the wholesaler has promised the seller to cover all closing and escrow costs. Daniels then stacks a one to two percent transactional origination fee on top [1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:09:48]. Jerry Norton shows that the fee does not shrink with speed: 2% on an $87,356 A to B leg is $1,747.12, even if the loan is repaid five minutes later [qWrqNQvtTO8 @ 00:02:23]. Jamil Damji flags the markets where the whole structure breaks. In high-price areas like California, Austin, San Francisco or Boston, medians run around $800,000. Seller policies scale with purchase price there, so the double close can cost more than the deal makes [KMD0dZIIYwc @ 00:04:37].

The remaining traps are operational, and they hit after the deal looks locked. Fuel My Deal names the core exposure plainly. If the end buyer backs out, the wholesaler can be stuck. If timelines get pushed, fees may increase. And not every title company is double close friendly [y5I0Ma11ptA @ 00:02:06]. Michael of The Virtual Investor quantifies the overrun. The Virtual Investor charges a flat fee or a percentage, plus 12% annualized interest once a deal slips past the one-to-three-day window. On that schedule, a $150,000 loan runs $3,000 plus about $50 a day [kCbwtS3VKw4 @ 00:07:16]. Jamil Damji warns that some title companies refuse assignments outright because two escrows pay them double the closing costs. That forces a double escrow whether the operator wanted one or not [KMD0dZIIYwc @ 00:05:27]. Dave Dinkle of LearnREInvesting adds a money-handling trap. Transactional and end-buyer funds must hit the closing agent's escrow account by wire only, because counterfeit money orders and cashier's checks are easy to produce on high quality copiers. Closing agents will not accept cash [gCae6AF4TSo @ 00:00:52]. The funder releases money only after reviewing both closing statements and confirming that the buyer's money has cleared.

callout.title: Pre-Close Kill Switch Checks
callout.body: Run these four checks before choosing between assigning, double escrowing, or funding the A to B leg. Each one comes from a loss, a squeeze, or a blown closing that operators reported firsthand.
items: Lock the B to C contract before calling a funder. Transactional lenders review both the purchase and the sale agreement, and they wire only when both sides of the transaction are complete [Jamil Damji — bnkxqdwWmdQ @ 00:00:38].

Price the double close as two full closings. That means two sets of title work, possibly title insurance on each leg, recording fees, transfer taxes on each deed, and the transactional funding fee, all on an itemized estimate [Odardo LLC — aHsBrb_hBYw @ 00:02:25].

Confirm the title company or closing attorney actually does double escrows. Some do and some do not, and operators can ask local fix-and-flip groups which escrow officers handle them [Brent Daniels - Wholesaling Inc — 1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:03:10].

Budget for slippage. If the deal does not close in the agreed time frame, additional fees and interest get expensive, and some lenders extend terms only at a higher rate [The Virtual Investor — kCbwtS3VKw4 @ 00:05:58].

chapters.pull_quote: "Good deals die because of timing, not because of math." — Sure Flow Capital Partners (sXh1jFRArig @ 00:00:40)
action_checklist: On direct-to-seller contracts, write your name followed by and or assigns so you can transfer your rights to a cash buyer without showing up at closing [Lex Levinrad Real Estate Training and Coaching — ogZEBPqsJc4 @ 00:01:15].

Call two title companies and ask four questions: whether they close assignments, whether they close double closes, how each leg must be funded, and what the itemized cost estimate is. Log every answer in a spreadsheet [Odardo LLC — aHsBrb_hBYw @ 00:06:39].

Set a fee rule before the deal goes live: assign under $15,000, and double escrow or double close above it, as long as costs are not chewing through the profit [Brent Daniels - Wholesaling Inc — 1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:12:25].

Source a local transactional funder instead of a big national company. Then use your closing track record to push the origination fee down toward roughly $1,000 [Brent Daniels - Wholesaling Inc — 1CnG4yCPR4M @ 00:05:22].

Get the property under contract, submit the deal to a transactional funder for review, coordinate the funder with the title company, then close and collect the spread [Sure Flow Capital Partners — AsVTF7HImUo @ 00:04:33].

Negotiate the purchase price down on the front end, for example $97,000 instead of $100,000, to absorb roughly $3,000 in transactional funding and transfer tax costs [Gerald Harris — 0Nli9p7r9jI @ 00:05:23].

chapters.question_prompt: What does transactional funding really cost, what terms should I expect, and how do I avoid overpaying or picking the wrong funder?
chapters.title: Transactional Funding Costs, Terms & Lender Selection
chapters.subtitle: Transaction fees and 1%-range pricing, rate comparisons, upfront and application fees, how long the money can stay in, extended transactional funding, seller-carryback deals, why some closing agents resist it, how lenders differ, what funders require, and real net-profit deal examples
chapters.executive_summary: Funders and wholesalers agree that transactional funding is same-day capital that sits inside escrow. It funds the A-to-B purchase and is repaid from the B-to-C sale. Funders skip the credit check, income verification and underwriting as long as a contracted end buyer exists. The street price clusters around 1% of the A-to-B amount. Velocity Advantage Capital charges 1% or less, and Dave Dinkel calls anything above 1% overpaying. The Full Deal REI shows a 1.5% fee on $150,000 costing $2,250, which grows to $3,750 when two title companies or a rushed close add roughly another point. The traps are junk fees for entry, processing and cancellation, plus minimums as high as $1,795. Practitioners split on whether 30-to-90-day extended funding counts as transactional funding at all, and on whether price or execution should drive lender selection.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every funder here describes the same core product. It is short-term capital dropped into one specific closing so the A-to-B purchase can fund before the B-to-C resale pays out. Sure Flow Capital Partners calls it partnering with a funding source for money that often never leaves escrow, and insists the operator is not a borrower but the person running the deal [2OXgeuq7LZU @ 00:00:01]. The same channel spells out the order-of-operations snag. The end buyer pays minutes later, but real money still has to fund the first leg. That money moves in and out the same day, sometimes within hours, and the operator keeps the spread minus closing costs and fees [2OXgeuq7LZU @ 00:01:20]. The Full Deal REI calls it borrowing for an afternoon. The funding usually covers the full purchase price and often the first-side closing costs, with both closings typically at the same title company on the same day [H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:00:47]. Dave Dinkel of LearnREInvesting adds the timing discipline. In some states the closing agent escrows both sides until every document and dollar is in place, and court orders or city inspections can delay a closing for days or months. The funder should still wire only on the day of the final closing, which is why the product gets called flash funding or one-day funding [sZe_QRsB_NE @ 00:00:29].

The second point of agreement is what the funder does not ask for. Cortez of Veteran Innovative Lending, speaking on Fund My Real Estate Deal, says flatly that it is not a traditional loan. There is typically no credit check, no income verification and no underwriting, as long as the contracts are in place and every party understands how the deal works. Cortez's overriding goal is that the lender's money never goes hard, which mitigates most of the risk [a--96aHg5xs @ 00:01:59]. The Full Deal REI confirms that most funders skip credit pulls, bank statements and tax returns because the closing itself repays them the same day. Some will even issue proof of funds for the double close when a seller or listing agent wants to see that the wholesaler can perform [H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:05:28]. Dinkel's Tennessee offer reads like a spec sheet for the same idea: 100% financing of the A-to-B price, proof of funds provided, no appraisal, no LTV or ARV calculation, no minimum fee, no processing fee and a simple one-page funding agreement [BbugvWp8qsA @ 00:00:00]. The one condition nobody bends on, per Dinkel, is an end buyer under contract to purchase the property after the first transaction closes [a0yQnepWIA4 @ 00:01:54].

The practitioners also agree on when a double close is worth paying for. The Full Deal REI is blunt that assigning is usually cheaper and lists four triggers for transactional funding. The first is a no-assignment clause, which is common on bank-owned REO deals and short sales. The second is an end buyer who refuses an assignment or wants the wholesaler on title for a clean chain. The third is state rules that make assignments harder or riskier. The fourth is a fee so large that printing it on an assignment invites the buyer to renegotiate [H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:03:54]. Dinkel draws the profit line with a number. The team generally keeps an assigned profit below fifteen thousand dollars, because above that the seller or end buyer may change their mind and the deal dies [VGIfE33jspg @ 00:01:03]. Dinkel prices the fix as slightly less than twice the first closing, which is small compared to losing the deal [VGIfE33jspg @ 00:01:20]. The Velocity Advantage Capital founder ran double closings locally in Charlotte, North Carolina, and describes the pain that pushed them into lending. Funder requirements changed every deal, capital was sometimes unavailable, and fees swung between 3% and 4%, all of it hitting the wholesaler's bottom line [HGfRd2Z2i24 @ 00:00:19].

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Dinkel breaks the bill into line items. The funding fee is a percentage of the lender funds actually sent to the A-to-B closing, so one hundred thousand dollars at 1% costs one thousand dollars. On top of that sits a wire fee that varies with the lender's bank. Then comes the minimum fee, which on amounts under thirty thousand dollars ranges from $350 to $1,795. Dinkel also flags three junk fees to hunt for. The first is a non-refundable fee to enter the lender's system. The second is a cancellation fee charged when the deal dies, even if no money moved. The third is a processing fee that is just the entry fee renamed [AvFYUxl4Gx8 @ 00:00:33]. Dinkel's ceiling is to never pay more than 1% of the A-to-B funds unless the lender negotiates lower or the deal needs over one million dollars [AvFYUxl4Gx8 @ 00:01:22]. A separate cost breakdown from Dinkel quotes funding fees of 1% to 2%, usually negotiated on closings of one million dollars or more. That breakdown lists minimums of $350 to $1,495 and cancellation fees of $399 to $750. Dinkel says only the funding, wire and minimum fees are what an investor should expect to pay [6muHPduCEtc @ 00:00:15]. On points, two points on one hundred thousand dollars is two thousand dollars, which Dinkel books as a cost of doing business for the investor [sZe_QRsB_NE @ 00:01:31].

The Full Deal REI runs a labeled example with a $150,000 A-to-B purchase, a $185,000 B-to-C sale and a $35,000 gross spread. At an example fee of 1.5%, the funder takes $2,250 straight out of the spread at closing. Two full sets of title work, settlement fees and possible transfer taxes come out after that [H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:02:08]. The hidden leak is setup. Two different title companies, or a rushed and messy closing, can add roughly another 1%, pushing the cost to 2.5%. That is $3,750, of which $1,500 is lost to poor coordination [H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:03:00]. Cortez uses the identical $150,000-to-$185,000 frame. The funder puts $150,000 in escrow, the end buyer's wire repays the $150,000 plus the fee, and the wholesaler keeps $35,000 minus that fee [a--96aHg5xs @ 00:02:35]. Dinkel's rate comparison converts percentages into dollars on a $200,000 double close: 3/4 of 1% is $1,500, 1% is $2,000, 1.5% is $3,000 and 2% is $4,000. A half point is $1,000 on one deal, and a full point is $2,000. Dinkel says a large Georgia wholesaler who only occasionally double closes would have saved over $100,000 in funding costs with that comparison chart [0u7L7Q7CE5o @ 00:01:11].

The intake process is deliberately routine. Velocity Advantage Capital sends a link with a short Q&A covering business name, contact details, property address and closing company. The request lands in their CRM, and an intro email goes out usually within an hour or two and definitely within 24 hours [Fb1_zsDd4XE @ 00:00:40]. In a second walkthrough, the founder quotes 10 to 15 minutes for that email, at a rate of 1% or less on every deal [HGfRd2Z2i24 @ 00:02:15]. From there the funder works directly with the title company or closing attorney. Near closing, the wholesaler signs a few confirmation-of-process and fee documents. On closing day the funder wires to the closing company and recovers principal plus fee on the second closing [Fb1_zsDd4XE @ 00:01:26]. Cortez stretches the same capital into adjacent plays. One is funding earnest money, which can reach 1% of the price as wholesaling laws change, or five to ten thousand dollars in some cases. The other is bridging the stack method. On a $100,000 purchase, the funder brings the 20% down payment, and a seller carry of 30% repays that 20% plus an extra 10%, so the buyer walks out of closing with cash [a--96aHg5xs @ 00:04:57].

callout.title: Spread Protection Moves From The Funding Desk
callout.body: These are the moves the funders and wholesalers use to keep fees from eating the spread and to keep the deal alive through closing day.
items: Compare net dollar costs, not percentages. Check the minimum fee, because it can dominate smaller A-to-B transactions, and confirm exactly which funding amount the percentage applies to [LearnREInvesting — 0u7L7Q7CE5o @ 00:02:10].

Use one title company for both sides, and build the funding fee plus two sets of closing costs into your numbers before you sign with the seller, not after [The Full Deal REI — H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:03:17].

Require a meaningful non-refundable deposit from your end buyer, with a clause letting escrow release it to you if the buyer fails to close, so their skin in the game covers your EMD [The Full Deal REI — H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:06:18].

Watch where the profit lands on the settlement statement. In one deal the listing agent put the student's profit on the second page of the HUD, so the seller saw no profit on page one [LearnREInvesting — 2MOHSWLCCqc @ 00:02:08].

sop_steps.title: Lock Both Contracts With Matching Names
sop_steps.action: Get the A-to-B and B-to-C contracts signed by all parties, with identical names and property address on both, and confirm the spread covers the fee and both sets of closing costs.
sop_steps.detail: Funders want both contracts signed, matching names and address, enough spread to absorb the funding fee and every closing cost, and same-day closings; if the math is too tight they pass [The Full Deal REI — H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:04:53].

sop_steps.title: Interview The Funder And Get Terms In Writing
sop_steps.action: Call a real representative and run the full question list: excluded states, upfront fees, dead-deal charges, minimum, funding fee, wire fee, back-end fees, extended closings, notice needed, and EMD funding.
sop_steps.detail: Dinkel says asking these questions also shows how cooperative the funder will be when things go wrong near closing [LearnREInvesting — l-l8leRQ_KE @ 00:00:31]. Dinkel also says to get the final fee and funding conditions in writing before the closing package is finalized [LearnREInvesting — 0u7L7Q7CE5o @ 00:02:48].

sop_steps.title: Submit Intake And Hand Off To The Closer
sop_steps.action: Fill out the funder's intake form with business details, property address, and the title company or closing attorney, then introduce the funder to whoever handles the closing.
sop_steps.detail: Velocity says the investor only needs to introduce the funder to the closing company, and the funder works with them directly until closing day instead of chasing the wholesaler for weeks or months [Velocity Advantage Capital — Fb1_zsDd4XE @ 00:00:57].

sop_steps.title: Fund The A-To-B And Recover On The B-To-C
sop_steps.action: Make sure the end buyer's funds are with the title company, let the funder wire the A-to-B, close both legs, and collect the spread after the funder is repaid.
sop_steps.detail: The funder usually will not wire until the buyer's money is sitting with the title company [The Full Deal REI — H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:05:09]. On the second closing, the funder gets its principal and fee back and the investor keeps the profit [Velocity Advantage Capital — Fb1_zsDd4XE @ 00:01:42].

sections.heading: 3. Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is price. Velocity Advantage Capital built its whole pitch around frustration with funders who charged 3% one deal and 4% the next, and now quotes a flat 1% or less on every deal with the same process each time [HGfRd2Z2i24 @ 00:00:55]. Dave Dinkel of LearnREInvesting draws a harder line: in no case should a wholesaler pay more than 1% of the A-to-B funds unless the lender negotiates lower or the amount needed tops one million dollars [AvFYUxl4Gx8 @ 00:01:22]. The Full Deal REI deliberately refuses to quote a live price and instead models 1.5% on a $150,000 purchase, a $2,250 hit straight out of the spread before the wholesaler sees a dime [H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:02:08]. Dinkel's comparison of the 13 most active funders converts those percentages into dollars on a $200,000 double close: 0.75% is $1,500, 1% is $2,000, 1.5% is $3,000 and 2% is $4,000, so a single point swings $2,000 on one deal [0u7L7Q7CE5o @ 00:00:50]. Yet the same comparison warns against picking off a single printed percentage, arguing that the funder's ability to execute the specific transaction, minimums and add-ons matter as much as the headline rate.

Practitioners also split on what the product even is. Sure Flow Capital Partners insists transactional funding is not a loan: the wholesaler is the operator, not a borrower, and the money generally never leaves escrow or follows anyone for 30 years [2OXgeuq7LZU @ 00:02:00]. Dave Dinkel openly calls it a very short-term loan for the purchase of a property, usually in effect for less than one or two hours [VGIfE33jspg @ 00:00:15]. The bigger fight is over duration. In one episode Dinkel says lenders advertising 30, 60 or even 90-day transactional funding are not really offering transactional funding at all, because they charge points plus interest for the extended period, while true transactional funding carries only points and ancillary fees [sZe_QRsB_NE @ 00:01:15]. In another episode Dinkel embraces extended transactional funding as a short-term loan of up to 90 days, built for REO closings where the bank's closing agent almost never allows a double close, short sales carrying 30-to-180-day deed restrictions, and foreclosure or tax deed auction wins that must be paid by cashier's check by noon the following day [a0yQnepWIA4 @ 00:00:14]. The operator takeaway is to name the product precisely: same-day flash funding and a multi-week hold are priced and structured differently.

Whether to double close at all is the third fault line. The Full Deal REI says that if you can assign, assigning is usually cheaper, and reserves double closes for no-assignment clauses common on REO and short sales, end buyers who want the wholesaler on title, state rules that make assignments riskier, and fat fees that make buyers renegotiate once they see the profit [H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:03:32]. Dave Dinkel puts a number on that last trigger, generally keeping assigned profit below $15,000 and accepting a double close cost that runs slightly less than twice the first closing because it is small compared to losing the deal [VGIfE33jspg @ 00:01:03]. Lenders pushing wider playbooks go further. The 22-year Air Force veteran behind Fund My Real Estate Deal funds earnest money deposits that can reach 1% of the purchase price, sometimes five to ten thousand dollars, as wholesaling laws change [a--96aHg5xs @ 00:00:42]. Sure Flow Capital Partners uses transactional money to satisfy the down payment a DSCR lender wants to see on a seller carryback, also called the stack or Morby method, so creative structures do not fall apart at the finish line [9HWpfZS4eQM @ 00:01:18].

sections.heading: 4. Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is paying for nothing. Dave Dinkel flags so-called junk fees: an entry fee into the lender's system that is non-refundable if the deal dies, which matters because a high percentage of deals do not close for reasons the investor never controlled, plus cancellation fees charged even when the lender never sent a dollar [AvFYUxl4Gx8 @ 00:00:49]. In a companion breakdown, Dinkel prices those cancellation fees at $399 to $750 and labels the administrative fee a pure additional profit source for the lender [6muHPduCEtc @ 00:00:32]. Dinkel's position is that there should never be any upfront cost for transactional funding, yet some lenders charge an application fee just to decide whether they will fund at all [l-l8leRQ_KE @ 00:00:00]. The Full Deal REI treats big upfront application fees as a walk-away red flag, along with 24-hour deadline pressure, proof of funds letters sold as a product with no real money behind them, no verifiable reviews or track record, and a title company that has never heard of the funder [H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:06:51]. The common defense: interview a live representative and get the final fee in writing before the closing package is finalized.

The second failure point is the closing table itself. Dave Dinkel reports that some closing agents hate transactional funding: conventional-loan veterans who will not bend their regulator-driven checklists even for cash buyers, attorneys who close real estate as a sideline between traffic tickets and criminal cases, and end-buyer attorneys who treat every investor as a criminal, including one who demanded to see the closing agent's escrow account holding the funder's money before releasing the client's wire [PlXZzAIYwfI @ 00:02:07]. Dinkel also reports being called in more than a few times to save closings wrecked by an inexperienced or inflexible funder, and swapping the closing agent means restarting title work and getting both the seller and end buyer to agree [6muHPduCEtc @ 00:01:21]. Velocity Advantage Capital's founder hit a different wall while double closing in Charlotte, North Carolina: requirements changed every time, nobody was dependable, and sometimes funders simply had no capital available [HGfRd2Z2i24 @ 00:00:36]. REO purchases add another hard stop, because the bank's chosen closing agent will almost never allow a double close, forcing the B-to-C leg elsewhere on another day [a0yQnepWIA4 @ 00:00:14]. Dinkel's fix is blunt: get referrals for investor-friendly closing agents and handle the end buyer's attorney as the issue presents itself.

The third trap is math done too late. The Full Deal REI shows how two title companies or a rushed, messy closing can add roughly another 1% on top of a 1.5% fee, lifting the cost to 2.5%, or $3,750 on a $150,000 purchase, which is $1,500 gone from poor setup; the rule is one title company for both sides and funding costs built in before signing with the seller [H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:03:00]. The same channel locates the real risk in the wholesaler's earnest money: demand a meaningful non-refundable deposit from the end buyer with an escrow release clause, and favor cash, private money and hard money buyers because FHA's ninety-day resale rule can block a fast flip [H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:06:34]. Dave Dinkel adds that FHA underwriting cannot even begin until the investor is recorded on title, so a financed end buyer typically needs four to eight weeks [a0yQnepWIA4 @ 00:02:10]. The stakes compound across volume: a large Georgia wholesaler who mostly assigns but occasionally double closes told Dinkel that the comparison chart would have saved over $100,000 in funding costs over the past years [0u7L7Q7CE5o @ 00:00:16]. Funding cost belongs in the offer price, not in a closing-day surprise.

callout.title: Kill the Funder or the Deal Before Closing Day
callout.body: Practitioner-reported pitfalls that should stop a double close before a single wire is requested.
items: Walk if the funder demands a big upfront application fee or pushes a 24-hour funding deadline, and confirm your title company has heard of them [The Full Deal REI — H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:06:51].

Get the total expected funding charge on the actual A-to-B amount in writing, including wire, processing, document rush, extended hold and split title company fees [LearnREInvesting — 0u7L7Q7CE5o @ 00:02:30].
If the spread cannot absorb the funding fee plus two sets of closing costs, it is not a double close deal [The Full Deal REI — H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:03:17].
Lock a non-refundable end buyer deposit with an escrow release clause before your own earnest money is exposed [The Full Deal REI — H-3pmQVYvCI @ 00:06:18].

action_checklist: Interview a live funder representative with the full question list: excluded states, upfront fees, cost if the deal dies, minimum, wire fee, back-end fees, extended closings and notice needed [LearnREInvesting — l-l8leRQ_KE @ 00:00:15].

Submit the deal through the funder's intake form with business details, property address and closing company, then hand the funder off to the title company or closing attorney [Velocity Advantage Capital — Fb1_zsDd4XE @ 00:00:20].

chapters.question_prompt: What do title companies, closing attorneys, and escrow actually do from contract to close, and how do I read the closing paperwork?
chapters.title: Title, Escrow & the Settlement Statement
chapters.subtitle: Title vs. escrow, wholesaler-friendly title companies and closing attorneys, the 10 closing steps, contract-to-close escrow, ALTA settlement statement vs. HUD-1 vs. Closing Disclosure, who pays closing costs, and the final funding and recording step for buyers and sellers
chapters.executive_summary: Wholesalers and closing-side operators converge on one control rule: the investor picks a wholesaler-friendly title company, opens escrow the day the contract is signed, and has title call the seller fast, because outside shops have branded assignments a scam and killed deals. Jerry Norton estimates about 25% of deals die on title issues and shows a $206,000 contract assigned at $231,000 for a $25,000 fee in two weeks, locked by a $5,000 non-refundable buyer deposit. Rick drills fee hygiene: lien searches billed at $75 to $250, padded junk charges, and a 50 to 55% reissue credit on quick resales. Escrow pros insist on phone-verified wires and recording before keys. The split runs over whether to expose the assignment fee on the buyer's statement, hide it from the seller with a blind HUD, or double close with transactional funding.
