sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every wholesaler working these closings lands on the same rule: whoever picks the title company controls the deal. Jerry Norton of Flipping Mastery TV lost a contract when a seller insisted on a preferred title shop that received Norton's assignment agreement, had no idea what to do with it, and told the seller it was a scam, so the seller canceled [3aAzZildhKk @ 00:02:53]. Norton's fix is a contract clause stating the seller agrees to use the buyer's title of choice; on agent-listed deals Norton calls the agent's title company, quizzes it on wholesale experience, and sticks to a preferred shop at any hint of doubt [3aAzZildhKk @ 00:05:08]. Jamil Damji reports a near-identical blowup: after letting a seller choose title, the escrow officer phoned the seller to say the buyer was trying to do something illegal, the seller feared jail, and the deal unraveled [_4J_JXkaaMg @ 00:04:52]. Rick of Flip With Rick calls title selection non-negotiable, traces most deals that died at a closing table back to an outside title company, would most likely walk away rather than concede, and warns that a supposedly neutral title company gives its loyalty and fastest communication to whoever brought it the deal [itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:05:08].

The second point of agreement is speed: send the executed contract to title the day it is signed, not after a buyer appears. Norton opens escrow right away because a seller who is not on title or a stack of back taxes can block the sale, and Norton puts the damage at about 25% of deals never reaching closing because of title issues [3aAzZildhKk @ 00:04:22]. Rick calls waiting for a cash buyer before submitting a really bad decision: a small title problem found late can push a deal from 30 days out to 90 or 120, while most problems get resolved in the first two to four weeks when caught early, and most title companies will eat a pull or two on dead deals for a steady client [itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:10:47]. Eric of Propy cites the American Land Title Association figure that about 36% of transactions need extensive work to clear title, roughly one in three deals [hn4wyDTnTXc @ 00:00:56]. Heather Jackson of Secure Title, training Realtypath agents, wants title ordered the moment a listing is taken; one early pull showed four owners instead of two, the extra pair being minor children who could not convey, which forced a court order [XlKk96ekJTE @ 00:22:20].

Practitioners also agree on what the closing shop actually does. Eric of Propy boils it down to title as the investigator proving the house is really the seller's to sell, and escrow as the referee holding money and documents until every contract condition is met, so nobody gets paid early and nobody gets the house early [hn4wyDTnTXc @ 00:03:03]. Rick frames a title company as an insurance company first: it underwrites each property, refuses a policy when it cannot get clean title, and keeps roughly 50 to 65% of the premium, so a $1,000 policy nets it $500 to $600 while the rest feeds an underwriting risk pool, which pushes cleaner shops to run a tighter ship [itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:02:01]. Jamil Damji maps the geography: in Phoenix the title company is also the escrow company, in California title and escrow are separate organizations, and in Georgia closing attorneys do the work of both [_4J_JXkaaMg @ 00:01:55]. Whatever the setup, everything lands on the settlement statement, which True Title calls the statement of accounting for the closing, reflecting all money changing hands, payments, credits, debits, and adjustments, and ending with an amount due line the buyer must pay for closing [qsZtsUB4AFM @ 00:00:01].

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The wholesale assignment runs on a fixed five-step spine at the title company. Norton contracts the seller, opens escrow, finds a cash buyer, and executes an assignment; on a $100,000 contract assigned for $115,000, the buyer pays the seller $100,000 and the wholesaler earns a $15,000 fee off a one-page agreement [0A2TpKfV1Os @ 00:03:34]. The buyer then sends a substantial non-refundable earnest money deposit, typically $5,000, to the same title company, and on a live deal Norton contracted at $206,000, assigned at $231,000, and booked a $25,000 fee on a two-week close; the title agent on that call keeps buyers and sellers signing separately so they never meet at the office [0A2TpKfV1Os @ 00:06:25]. Title prepares separate statements so the seller sees only the seller side, while the assignment fee appears as a line item on the buyer's statement; to hide the fee from the buyer as well, Norton double closes and brings transactional funding [3aAzZildhKk @ 00:07:26]. Jamil Damji gets the same seller-side privacy through a blind HUD, arguing that a seller who sees a $10,000 assignment fee asks why that money was not added to the price, when that spread is how wholesalers feed their families [_4J_JXkaaMg @ 00:07:05].

Rick's fee playbook starts with the lien search: most title companies charge $75 to $250, it typically costs them $50 to $100, so the fee is highly negotiable, and Rick insists on the written report because it has clawed back thousands of dollars when liens surfaced months or years after closing [itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:11:40]. Government charges are non-negotiable and earn title nothing, but settlement fees, lien search charges, and wire fees are fair game; Rick has been quoted a $395 settlement fee padded with $700 in junk charges and has seen $200 wire fees, so the move is to demand the total of every non-government fee while interviewing the company [itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:14:11]. On a double close or quick wholetail resale, Rick asks for the reissue credit, a 50 to 55% discount on the second title policy that cuts a $2,000 premium by at least $1,000 [itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:14:39]. The Suzanne & Chad Team anchors the Florida seller side: documentary stamp tax on the deed at 70 cents per $100 of value, an HOA estoppel and a municipal lien search each running around a couple hundred dollars, and title service fees from a couple hundred up to roughly $500 per side [ImGiAjG57s0 @ 00:02:30].

Statement mechanics trip up new operators. Molly Gilbert of Train Title, on Tony Zowd's channel, explains that the lender prepares the CD with one party per document, the title company prepares the ALTA with buyer and seller side by side, and the old HUD-1 still shows up on investment, commercial, and cash purchases; buyers should keep the ALTA because it shows ownership until the deed records [KmNl8nlbUxw @ 00:01:17]. Kim Fields of Title Scoop adds that the CD can display owner's and lender's title premiums confusingly because of how the CFPB requires them shown, while the ALTA shows exactly what each party pays, and the bottom lines of the two must match; reverse mortgages often still demand the HUD-1 [-L_sEB2gX4Y @ 00:00:55]. Heather Jackson sets the money rules: title accepts no cash, cashier's checks only under $10,000 and they must clear before same-day funding, so wire before the 3 PM Mountain cutoff; financed buyers need the CD three calendar days before settlement, cash buyers 24 hours [XlKk96ekJTE @ 01:03:08]. Adam Dobrinich closes the loop: escrow reconciles the file on recording day and sends seller wires or checks within one business day, sometimes the same day if recording happens early enough [SmGAUIMTEyI @ 00:02:31].

callout.title: Four Plays That Squeeze Cost, Time, and Risk Out of the Closing File
callout.body: Operators pull these levers inside the title file to cut fees, lock contracts, and close faster than the deal would close on its own.
items: Ask for the reissue credit on any double close or quick resale; title applies a 50 to 55% discount on the second-side policy only when asked [Flip With Rick — itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:14:39].

Call a title company's legal department and have the staff attorney hand over the assignment, double-close, and creative-deal documents the company is comfortable closing, free, because the company wants the business [Jamil Damji — _4J_JXkaaMg @ 00:10:26].
Write 'check or wire' in the earnest money delivery field of the contract so the form of payment can never be contested [Realtypath — XlKk96ekJTE @ 00:28:55].
Have the seller sign the notarized documents before a slow mortgage payoff arrives so the file can move to close the moment the payoff lands [Flipping Mastery TV — 0A2TpKfV1Os @ 00:10:20].

sop_steps.title: Lock the Closer and Open Escrow Day One
sop_steps.action: Send the executed seller contract and any earnest money to your chosen wholesaler-friendly title company immediately.
sop_steps.detail: Norton opens escrow right away to surface title problems early; close of escrow typically runs 30 days but can be 10 days to 2 weeks, and title fees are paid at closing rather than upfront, with Norton never paying for title work on a deal that did not close [Flipping Mastery TV — 0A2TpKfV1Os @ 00:02:42].

sop_steps.title: Trigger the Seller Welcome Call and Payoff Pull
sop_steps.action: Have title call the seller within 12 hours, never past 24, to verify contact details, mortgage, and liens.
sop_steps.detail: Rick says that title welcome call saves more wholesale deals than anything else [Flip With Rick — itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:09:02]; Heather Jackson adds that payoff authorizations need an actual signature, not a digital one, because local banks and credit unions reject e-signatures [Realtypath — XlKk96ekJTE @ 00:42:22].

sop_steps.title: Assign, Collect the Buyer Deposit, Split the Statements
sop_steps.action: Deliver the executed assignment to the same title company and require the buyer's non-refundable deposit there.
sop_steps.detail: Norton asks for $5,000 to commit the cash buyer and gives title both contracts so it can build separate seller and buyer statements [Flipping Mastery TV — 0A2TpKfV1Os @ 00:04:22]; Damji uses a blind HUD so the seller never sees the assignment fee [Jamil Damji — _4J_JXkaaMg @ 00:06:51].

sop_steps.title: Fund, Record, and Get Wired
sop_steps.action: Phone-verify wire instructions, fund the file, and let escrow release the deed to record before disbursing.
sop_steps.detail: Buyers call escrow to read back wire instructions before sending the remaining down payment and costs, and escrow releases the deed to record only after funding [Adam Dobrinich | East Bay Realtor — FLFrQtywQ5g @ 00:00:48]; Norton skips the closing and has title wire the assignment fee straight to Norton's account [Flipping Mastery TV — 0A2TpKfV1Os @ 00:12:40].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Control of the title desk is the sharpest split. Flip With Rick treats choosing the title company as non-negotiable and says that if the other side insists on its own shop, Rick would most likely walk away from the deal, because whoever picks title is in control and most of Rick's blown closings trace back to an outside title company [itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:05:08]. Jerry Norton on Flipping Mastery TV runs a softer play on listed deals: call the listing agent's preferred title company, quiz them on wholesale experience, and use them if they sound capable, only digging in and demanding a buyer's-choice clause when there is any doubt [3aAzZildhKk @ 00:05:22]. Jamil Damji lands on Rick's side after getting burned: letting a seller choose title once ended with the escrow officer telling the seller the buyer was trying to do something illegal [_4J_JXkaaMg @ 00:04:52]. Retail practice muddies the picture further. Suzanne & Chad report that in Broward County the buyer typically selects title and pays the owner's policy, while in Osceola County the seller picks title and pays that policy, so the default control point shifts county by county before anyone negotiates it [ImGiAjG57s0 @ 00:01:33].

How much of the spread the other parties see is the second fault line. Jerry Norton's assignment playbook accepts that the cash buyer sees the assignment fee as a line item on the buyer-side statement, and offers a double closing as the alternative that hides the fee but forces the wholesaler to come up with funds to close, known as transactional funding [3aAzZildhKk @ 00:07:26]. In the companion walkthrough, the same operator describes a double closing in escrow that uses the cash buyer's funds to fund both transactions, and notes the title company will more than likely build a separate closing statement so the seller sees only that side [0A2TpKfV1Os @ 00:05:24]. Jamil Damji leans on the blind HUD: citing privacy laws, the escrow officer keeps seller documents with the seller and buyer documents with the buyer, so sellers never see a $10,000 assignment fee and ask why that money did not go into their price, which Jamil Damji calls simply how wholesalers make money [_4J_JXkaaMg @ 00:06:51]. The title agent on Jerry Norton's live call adds a physical layer: buyers and sellers sign separately at different times, and that agent virtually never lets them run into each other at the office [0A2TpKfV1Os @ 00:08:41].

Practitioners also split on paperwork and deposit size. Tony Zowd's guest Molly Gilbert says retail buyers with a residential lender get a CD from the lender plus an ALTA from title, while investment, commercial, and cash buyers get the HUD-1 because it is the easiest all around [KmNl8nlbUxw @ 00:01:17]. Kim Fields of Title Scoop agrees the HUD-1 lives mostly in cash and commercial deals and reverse mortgages, but reports a movement toward the ALTA on cash transactions depending on where you are, and prefers the ALTA because the CD can blur who is actually paying the owner's and lender's title premium [-L_sEB2gX4Y @ 00:01:52]. On earnest money, Flip With Rick tells wholesalers to post whatever the contract says, anywhere from $100 to $1,000 or even a $10 deposit, refundable based on the inspection period, mainly so the seller knows the buyer is serious; skip the deposit and the seller starts talking to Realtor friends who note no deposit was left, which is when contracts start to slip [itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:07:34]. Jerry Norton flips the pressure onto the end buyer instead, demanding a substantial non-refundable deposit of $5,000 or higher, which the cash buyer forfeits if they flake out, something Jerry Norton says happens more than you think [3aAzZildhKk @ 00:06:22].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure is a title desk that does not understand the deal. Jerry Norton lost a contract when a seller's preferred title company received the assignment agreement, had no idea what to do with it, and told the seller it was a scam, so the seller canceled; that burn is why Jerry Norton's contracts now say the seller agrees to use the buyer's title of choice [3aAzZildhKk @ 00:02:53]. Jamil Damji's deal died the same way: after the seller picked title, the escrow officer called the seller to say the buyer was trying to do something illegal, the seller feared jail and a fraudulent transaction, and Jamil Damji chose not to force the issue, so everything fell apart [_4J_JXkaaMg @ 00:05:07]. Defects in the public record are the next killer. Propy cites the American Land Title Association figure that about 36% of transactions, roughly one in three, need extensive work to clear title before closing [hn4wyDTnTXc @ 00:01:14]. Flip With Rick puts a clock on procrastination: wholesalers who wait for a cash buyer before submitting the contract can eat delays from 30 days up to 90 to 120 days when even a small title problem surfaces late, which is why Rick wants title pulled as soon as the contract is executed [itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:10:47].

Money movement is where files stall or vanish. Tom Olsewski insists on calling the escrow company a second time to verify wiring instructions before sending the deposit, and on a true wire rather than an ACH transfer [haXXzqITogY @ 00:01:08]. Adam Dobrinich repeats the drill at funding: when the buyer wires the rest of the down payment and closing costs, call escrow and have them read the instructions back [FLFrQtywQ5g @ 00:00:48]. Realtypath's Josh and Heather Jackson warn that stolen closing funds, once overseas, are very hard to recover even with the FBI involved, and clients can lose their savings or equity; they add that title will not take cash, a check only works under $10,000 with a wire above that, a cashier's check must clear deposit before same-day funding, and wires should land before the 3 PM Mountain cutoff [XlKk96ekJTE @ 01:03:30]. Payoffs and liens bite on the seller side. On Jerry Norton's live title call, a reverse mortgage sold to a company called Novad left the seller struggling to find payoff information, and title needed the original borrowers' Social Security numbers to chase it; the title agent still had the seller sign the notarized documents early so the file could close the moment the payoff arrived [0A2TpKfV1Os @ 00:07:20].

Paperwork gaps and timing assumptions are the quiet killers. Heather Jackson has balanced a lender CD showing seller-paid closing costs from addendum five while holding only addenda through three, and has prepared documents at a sales price that had since changed; Josh adds that an addendum not copied to escrow, lender, and the other side can send the file back through underwriting while the deadline looms and movers are already booked [XlKk96ekJTE @ 00:48:58]. Flip With Rick has had liens surface months or years after closing and says the paid lien search report is what forced title to work it out, bringing back thousands of dollars; skip the report and title says it checked but never ran an official search [itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:12:12]. Recording timing traps sellers and buyers alike. Adam Dobrinich will not hand over keys until the county confirms recording, which happens the same day only if the loan funds early enough [FLFrQtywQ5g @ 00:01:38], and on the seller side everything, including trash bags, must be out before the transaction records, a professional clean runs about a couple hundred dollars if the seller runs out of time, and proceeds go out by wire or check within one business day [SmGAUIMTEyI @ 00:01:08].

callout.title: Kill-Switch Checks Before Money or Paper Moves
callout.body: Four practitioner-tested checks that stop the failures above before they cost a deal, a deposit, or the closing funds.
items: Do not wire a dollar until the escrow company has been called a second time to verify the instructions directly, and send a true wire, never an ACH transfer [Tom Olsewski - Team Olsewski — haXXzqITogY @ 00:01:08].
Submit the executed contract and pull title immediately; waiting for a cash buyer can turn a small title defect into a 90 to 120 day delay [Flip With Rick — itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:10:47].
Lock the buyer's title of choice into the seller contract before any assignment lands on a desk that might call it a scam [Flipping Mastery TV — 3aAzZildhKk @ 00:03:07].

Commit or cancel before the 17th day of a 30-day escrow, because after that the seller has the right to keep the earnest money deposit as liquidated damages [Diana Cifuentes — eMR8CmhQHhk @ 00:04:02].

chapters.pull_quote: "Whoever picks the title company is really in control. It is the bottom line." — Flip With Rick (itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:05:08)
action_checklist: Send the fully executed contract to title the day it is signed and have title call the seller within 12 hours, never past 24, to welcome them and verify mortgage and lien information [Flip With Rick — itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:09:02].

Interview every title company on how many wholesale deals it closes monthly, and pull referrals from an active local investor Facebook group before committing [Flipping Mastery TV — 3aAzZildhKk @ 00:08:24].
Ask the title company's staff attorney for the assignment and double-close documents that title is comfortable using, then send that title company the business [Jamil Damji — _4J_JXkaaMg @ 00:10:26].
Pay for the lien search, demand the written report, and keep it alongside the title commitment in every deal file [Flip With Rick — itXS_PDnxa8 @ 00:12:41].
Walk the client through the settlement statement before the table, confirming who pays the home warranty, HOA transfer fees, and reinvestment fees [Realtypath — XlKk96ekJTE @ 00:56:39].
Confirm the bottom line of the CD and the ALTA settlement statement match before anyone signs [Title Scoop by Kim Fields — -L_sEB2gX4Y @ 00:01:36].

chapters.question_prompt: Where does earnest money go, when can it be lost, and how do buyers and wholesalers protect their deposit?
chapters.title: Earnest Money Deposits: Holding, Protecting & Losing Them
chapters.subtitle: What EMD is and where it's held, contingencies and inspection periods, state-specific rules (Florida, Connecticut, Idaho, New Jersey), wholesaler EMD practices, cancellation and refund scenarios, and e-tender EMD escrow
chapters.executive_summary: Realtors, attorneys, a mortgage lender and a wholesaler converge on one rule: the earnest money deposit sits with a neutral holder (title, a brokerage trust account, or attorney escrow) and becomes a closing credit. It is only recoverable through a live, written contingency. Inspection, loan, appraisal and title windows are the exits. Miss a date or waive a clause and the money is exposed. Street numbers run from a $1 consideration floor and a 1% Idaho resale reference to the 3% scripted benchmark, plus 10% deposits in Greenwich and on custom builds, and builder deposits that go hard at signing. The mechanics are three-day funding, wires sent only on title-direct instructions, 60-day fund seasoning, and daily deadline calls. Practitioners split on who holds the money, on whether release needs both sides to sign, and on wholesalers skipping deposits entirely.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus: Neutral Escrow, a Credit at Closing, and Contingencies as the Only Shield
paragraphs: Every practitioner who addresses custody agrees on one point: the deposit does not land in the seller's pocket. Katie Anderson in Pensacola sends it to the title company or the closing attorney. They park it in an escrow account tagged with the property address until the contract either cancels or closes [NMjK2yG_6ys @ 00:00:31]. Charles Nedder runs a different pipe in Greenwich, Connecticut. The buyer wires the deposit to the buyer's attorney, who forwards it with the signed contract to the seller's attorney. It then sits untouched in that attorney's escrow account [xyiyeiBkCqQ @ 00:00:47]. The Treasure Valley Home Show team in Idaho says the holder is always a neutral third party, either a brokerage trust account or title, and that title is now the usual landing spot [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:08:43]. On a clean close the money is neither a fee nor consumed. Lender Chase Hodson tells buyers to read it as a line on an accounting ledger: a credit that offsets closing costs or down payment [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:03:35]. Alec Osland of Yanowitz Law Firm states the same mechanic plainly. The deposit stays in a neutral escrow until closing and then gets applied toward the down payment or closing costs [D8jafo21-34 @ 00:00:57]. The operator takeaway is simple: the deposit is cash-to-close parked early, not a payment to the other side.

The second consensus is that contingencies are the only reliable way out with the money intact. Ed Kaminsky names three core protections: inspection, loan approval and appraisal. He says a buyer who is not satisfied with the outcome of any of them can cancel and take the deposit back [p5RGCN-UQL8 @ 00:00:46]. Daryl Williams of Win-Win Realtors adds a fourth, the preliminary title report contingency. He says a buyer who finds something they disapprove of during any of those windows is entitled to the refund [y9awo1XfRU4 @ 00:01:28]. The scripted agent pitch delivered by James Brinkman and his peers carries the same warning. Back out without a valid reason such as a contingency, and the seller may have the right to the deposit for breach of contract [NqrtD90l6pk @ 00:00:53]. Andrew Finney goes further and tells buyers to always leave the inspection contingency in place. That clause is what lets them walk and recover the deposit when a seller refuses to repair real defects [ND7J57hzroE @ 00:01:47]. JAG Real Estate's walkthrough of the California form shows how deep the exit menu runs. The loan, appraisal, property investigation, insurance, seller documents and title report all work as ways out that return the deposit [E9HjXJUTsZc @ 00:03:18].

Third, every speaker treats the calendar as the real battlefield. Charles Nedder says contract dates are not suggestions. They are the lines that decide whether the deposit is protected or exposed, and missing a deadline or waiving a contingency without understanding the risk leaves a buyer exposed [xyiyeiBkCqQ @ 00:03:38]. Katie Anderson gives the concrete version. A buyer with a 15-day right to inspect and cancel who changes their mind on day 20 has acted outside the contract, and that deposit should be released to the seller [NMjK2yG_6ys @ 00:01:41]. The Idaho agent says that as each contingency drops away, the earnest money moves deeper into jeopardy. A contingency can clear simply because the date passed [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:12:00]. The practitioners also agree that escrow holders will not pick a winner on their own. Robert Greenblatt in New Jersey says the escrow holder is not allowed to release the money unless both parties agree. A buyer who simply wants out after the inspection cannot just walk away with it [CCWuS-x3COc @ 00:01:39]. Anderson describes the endgame when nobody signs the release form. The funds sit in the title or attorney escrow account while the sides try to mediate, and in very rare cases the fight goes to court [NMjK2yG_6ys @ 00:02:41].

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools and Numbers: Sizing, Funding, Sourcing and Deadline Control
paragraphs: Sizing runs from a token dollar to a fifth of the price, depending on market and product. Robert Greenblatt says a New Jersey contract only needs consideration, so a deposit could technically be $1. In practice $1,000 often is not enough and some sellers want 10%. His test is behavioral: a buyer with $1,000 at risk may walk, while a buyer with $20,000 in escrow probably will not [CCWuS-x3COc @ 00:00:58]. Ed Kaminsky says the deposit is typically 3% of the purchase price. That figure is common because of the liquidated damages clause [p5RGCN-UQL8 @ 00:01:58]. The Idaho team uses roughly 1% as a reference point on resale homes, or $5,000 on a half-million-dollar house [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:20:58]. Builder contracts on custom homes are another story. They can demand 10% on a $600,000 to $1 million build, and the agent has heard of 20%, because the builder has already spent cash on a personalized product [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:34:22]. In Greenwich, Charles Nedder says local custom is 10% at contract signing. On a $2 million home that means wiring $200,000 to your attorney, often within five days of the accepted offer [xyiyeiBkCqQ @ 00:01:49]. At either end of that range, the cash has to be staged before the offer goes in, not scraped together after acceptance.

Delivery runs on a tight clock. Katie Anderson says page one of the contract states where the deposit goes and how many days the buyer has. Typically that is three business days to get it into escrow [NMjK2yG_6ys @ 00:00:15]. The Idaho agent says the state form defaults to three days, counted from the day after full ratification. An offer accepted on Monday means Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. The buyer must still fund on time even after spotting a problem, because funding is a contractual commitment [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:09:36]. Payment rails are narrow. Kim Haber says title companies take a wire transfer and some still take a cashier's check, but most now require a wire. Cash, debit and credit cards are not accepted [1ysRoNF77u8 @ 00:01:31]. Sourcing is the lender's hidden gate. Chase Hodson says cash pulled from a wall safe or mattress and deposited the day before is non-sourceable, because the funds must show in the account for 60 days. Gifts must be documented as non-repayable [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:19:20]. If the deposit cannot be sourced, the lender backs the credit out and the buyer has to replace it with sourceable funds [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:23:46]. JAG Real Estate says most parties want the deposit wired precisely so it can be tracked [E9HjXJUTsZc @ 00:02:39].

The operators who play offense work the contract terms themselves. In One Percent's wholesaling playbook, the investor funds the deposit to title only when no end buyer is lined up. Otherwise the end buyer sends it, and the investor gets the money back with the assignment fee. Sections four and five of his purchase agreement let him cancel by written notice, even a text or email, inside the inspection period, and the escrow agent then releases the deposit with no further written instructions [YO8RBYT_lQ0 @ 00:01:31]. He also scripts a no-deposit pitch to sellers: a deposit delays the process and limits the cash offer [YO8RBYT_lQ0 @ 00:03:19]. The Idaho agent cuts the all-contingencies-cleared clause from the seven-day default to one day before close to protect financed buyers [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:17:01]. On a 100% VA loan where the buyer cannot source cash, he writes a $500 deposit rather than let $5,000 appear out of nowhere [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:22:02]. Larry Mastropieri's team runs around 40 active deals and reads every contractual deadline aloud on an 8 a.m. operations call. When a seller asks for a 14-day loan commitment, his team gets the lender on the phone and makes them confirm it two or three times [CSHBzTZo3Yc @ 00:02:51]. JAG Real Estate says setting these timelines is how they have beaten multiple all-cash offers [E9HjXJUTsZc @ 00:10:51].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The deposit number itself is where operators split hardest. Kristie Dimarakis runs a flat 3% script, pegging a $650,000 offer at a $19,500 good faith deposit as the default way to show the seller you are serious about buying their home [NwZ7Oa8GUXQ @ 00:00:38]. The Treasure Valley team in Idaho works off roughly 1% on resale and spec homes, about $5,000 on a half-million-dollar house, and will deliberately write just $500 on a 100% VA deal when the buyer's account does not show the cash, rather than letting a borrowed $5,000 suddenly appear and trigger a sourcing fight later [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:22:02]. Charles Nedder sits at the opposite pole: Greenwich custom is 10% at contract signing, which means a $200,000 wire on a $2 million home, often within five days of an accepted offer, and the deal is not secure until that wire lands [xyiyeiBkCqQ @ 00:01:49]. Robert Greenblatt argues the dollar figure is legally trivial, since a New Jersey contract can technically be held with $1 of consideration, but psychologically decisive: a buyer with $1,000 at risk may walk the moment nerves hit, while a buyer with $20,000 sitting in escrow is far less likely to bail, so the amount itself sends the seller a commitment message [CCWuS-x3COc @ 00:00:58].

Operators also split on who sits on the money and what it takes to pry it loose. Katie Anderson routes Pensacola deposits to the title company or closing attorney within three business days, and warns that if the parties will not sign a release form even when the contract is clear, the funds sit in that escrow account through mediation and, rarely, court [NMjK2yG_6ys @ 00:02:41]. Charles Nedder runs it attorney-to-attorney: the buyer's attorney forwards the deposit with the signed contract to the seller's attorney, and once contingencies lapse both attorneys must agree before a cent moves [xyiyeiBkCqQ @ 00:03:07]. Robert Greenblatt states the escrow rule bluntly: the holder cannot release unless both parties agree, and a buyer who just wants out after inspection under the standard agreement of sale does not get an automatic refund, it becomes a negotiation [CCWuS-x3COc @ 00:01:39]. The One Percent wholesaling crew writes around that problem in their own paper: section five of their purchase and sale agreement says that if the buyer cancels during the inspection period, no further written instructions are required for the title company or title attorney to release the deposit back, no questions asked, which turns the refund into a paperwork formality [YO8RBYT_lQ0 @ 00:02:47].

The sharpest strategic split is whether to stretch contingency windows or compress them. The Treasure Valley team notes Idaho's default clears all contingencies seven days before close, so on a 30-day escrow a loan problem discovered on day 22 leaves the buyer exposed; their fix is to collapse that window to one day in their offers, while admitting a listing agent may push back because sellers want to know sooner [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:17:01]. Daryl Williams works the default 17-day review and 21-day loan periods, and if financing is not approved in time, asks for an extension and cancels outright if the listing side refuses [y9awo1XfRU4 @ 00:03:31]. JAG Real Estate Lifestyle plays the other direction: tighten every timeline using trusted vendors so the offer reads as good as cash, a method they say has beaten multiple all-cash offers, including on their own purchase [E9HjXJUTsZc @ 00:10:51]. Larry Mastropieri splits the difference when a seller demands a 14-day loan commitment: the team gets the lender on the phone, confirms the buyer can deliver documents by tomorrow, and makes an outside lender repeat two or three times that the deadline is a non-issue with no excuses [CSHBzTZo3Yc @ 00:02:51].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common way practitioners watch deposits die is a blown clock rather than a bad house. Katie Anderson lays out the textbook loss: a buyer with a 15-day right to inspect and cancel who changes their mind on day 20, or simply gets spooked by the inspection report, has walked outside the contract and the money should go to the seller [NMjK2yG_6ys @ 00:01:20]. The One Percent crew gives wholesalers the same math on a 14-day inspection period: let day 15 or 16 pass without canceling or finding a buyer and you are technically liable to hand that deposit to the seller, and you are not getting it back [YO8RBYT_lQ0 @ 00:02:05]. Daryl Williams adds the post-removal trap, warning that once you and your agent remove contingencies, a change of heart about the property for whatever reason means you say bye bye to your deposit [y9awo1XfRU4 @ 00:04:16]. The Treasure Valley team stresses that contingencies do not only clear when you sign them off; they clear just by missing the date, which is why their team runs a hyperdetailed, calendar-driven transaction coordinator so no deadline slips and the earnest money stays out of jeopardy [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:36:30].

The second killer is stripping protections in the heat of a bidding war. Andrew Finney has watched buyers in multiple-bid fights drop the loan contingency, then the inspection contingency, then everything, which leaves them on the hook for the house whether they can afford it or not; lose a job or get caught in a one-to-two-month transfer gap and the lender treats them as unqualified [ND7J57hzroE @ 00:03:05]. Finney also prices the appraisal waiver: on a $400,000 list price appraising at $390,000, waiving means agreeing upfront to pay $10,000 over appraised value instead of renegotiating or splitting the gap five and five [ND7J57hzroE @ 00:04:27]. Chase Hodson, the Treasure Valley lender, describes a colleague whose verbal verification of employment within 24 to 48 hours of signing revealed the borrower had lost their job, before the employer had even told the borrower, and the lender had to break the news at the signing table [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:14:36]. Ed Kaminski shows what an intact appraisal contingency buys: on a $1 million purchase appraising at $900,000, the buyer can cancel and recover the deposit, renegotiate the price, or bring more down payment and still close [p5RGCN-UQL8 @ 00:01:06].

The last cluster of losses happens outside the contingency calendar entirely. Chase Hodson warns that cash pulled from a wall safe or mattress and deposited the day before the earnest money wire is still nonsourceable, because lenders on conventional, FHA, USDA and Fannie or Freddie backed loans want 60 days of history; if the deposit cannot be sourced, that credit gets backed out and must be replaced with funds under the same scrutiny, so the fix is to bank the cash 60 days before going under contract [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:24:01]. The Treasure Valley host flags wire fraud: scammers send emails that look identical to title, so wire only on instructions straight from the title company, call them yourself, and know that once five grand is intercepted it can kill the deal [5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:38:50]. Charles Nedder notes that a disputed release after contingencies expire keeps the deposit frozen in escrow until both attorneys agree or a court decides, a process that can take months [xyiyeiBkCqQ @ 00:03:22]. JAG Real Estate Lifestyle hands every buyer a wire fraud advisory alongside the investigation advisory for exactly that reason, with an instruction to call the team if anything about transferring money is unclear [E9HjXJUTsZc @ 00:07:19].

callout.title: Four Checks Before Any Deposit Goes At Risk
callout.body: Every loss these operators reported traces back to a missed date, a stripped contingency, unsourced cash, or a hijacked wire. Clear all four before money moves.
items: Calendar every contractual deadline at ratification and cancel in writing by day nine or ten of a 10-day inspection period; Mastropieri's team reads all deadlines aloud at an 8 a.m. operations call across roughly 40 live deals [Larry Mastropieri — CSHBzTZo3Yc @ 00:01:27].
Never drop the loan contingency to win a multiple-bid fight, because without it the buyer is on the hook for the house whether they can afford it or not [Andrew Finney Team — ND7J57hzroE @ 00:03:18].

Move any cash into a bank account 60 days before going under contract so the earnest money is sourceable and the closing credit is not backed out [The Treasure Valley Home Show — 5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:19:20].

Wire only on instructions that came directly from the title company and confirm them by calling title yourself, since intercepted funds are gone [The Treasure Valley Home Show — 5lKK7iczAKk @ 00:38:18].

chapters.pull_quote: 'The contract is what protects your deposit. Not a handshake, not a verbal agreement, not an assumption that things will work out.' — Charles Nedder | Greenwich CT Real Estate (xyiyeiBkCqQ @ 00:03:38).
action_checklist: Get the earnest money into the title company or closing attorney's escrow account within the contract window, typically three business days from acceptance [Katie Anderson | PENSACOLA AREA REALTOR — NMjK2yG_6ys @ 00:00:15].
Confirm payment options with your agent and escrow officer and send a wire transfer or cashier's check, never cash, debit, or credit [Kristie Dimarakis — NwZ7Oa8GUXQ @ 00:02:01].

Write financing, inspection, and appraisal contingencies into the purchase agreement as the legal escape clauses that return the deposit [Yanowitz Law Firm, PLLC │ Will & Trust Lawyers — D8jafo21-34 @ 00:01:15].

On the inspection response, leave cosmetic items like paint and carpet at the door and push the seller on HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and water heater straps [Andrew Finney Team — ND7J57hzroE @ 00:02:01].
If the loan is not approved inside the 21-day period, request an extension, and cancel the agreement if the listing side refuses [Win-Win Realtors TV — y9awo1XfRU4 @ 00:03:31].

Have your attorney review every deadline and every contingency before you sign, because those dates decide whether the deposit is protected or exposed [Charles Nedder | Greenwich CT Real Estate — xyiyeiBkCqQ @ 00:03:22].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I show proof of funds without having the cash, and what money risks around closing—tax prorations and wire fraud—can blow up the numbers?
chapters.title: Proof of Funds, Prorations & Wire Fraud
chapters.subtitle: Free and lender-issued proof of funds letters for cash offers, transactional-funding POF, property tax and HOA prorations that change closing math, unpaid property taxes, and how buyers and title companies fend off wire fraud
chapters.executive_summary: Wholesalers and closers converge on one rule: the money has to look real before contract and move clean at settlement. Brent Daniels pulls free proof-of-funds letters from local hard money lenders, doubleclose.com and besttransactionalfunding.com; Jerry Norton says about 90% of agents accept a soft letter and the rest get a five-to-seven-day contingency; Steph Davis used a father's line-of-credit statement and Tailwind letters at $1.99 each or $9.99 a month. Transactional lenders fund 100% of A-to-B legs, often within hours. At closing, Matthew Halliday and Julee Felsman break prorations into daily math, 14-month escrow cushions and 115% hold-and-pay collections. Title and escrow operators warn wires are gone once sent, citing $160,000 and $250,000 losses. The split: Norton fires agents who reject soft letters, while Davis downgrades to a financed offer.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Proof of funds is a listing-side checkpoint, and every wholesaler on the board treats it that way. Flipping Mastery TV says the request almost always comes from agents, because most sellers never think to ask unless somebody educates them, and the operator deliberately educates sellers on what a viable buyer and contract look like to stand out from loose, one-sided wholesale paper [9NXVYf_SZCA @ 00:00:00]. Steph Davis of FlipThisWholesaler draws the same line by deal type: private, unlisted sellers typically skip the request and accept a smaller earnest money deposit, while bank-owned listings and short sales almost always demand a letter with a cash offer, and savvy investor-sellers may ask for both a bigger deposit and proof [FOfp5iWKVkc @ 00:01:19]. Brent Daniels frames the letter as the thing agents and owners are screening for, since nothing frustrates them more than a buyer who submits offers and cannot close, and Daniels says the wholesaler enters every deal as the cash buyer on the purchase agreement until the contract is assigned [AcL3tusr27o @ 00:04:43]. Jerry Norton adds the strategic payoff: an all-cash offer jumps ahead of every financing-contingency offer, and a letter attached to it makes the agent and seller feel the offer is legitimate [R83ectOeUdU @ 00:01:41].

The second point of agreement is that a cash offer does not require the buyer's own cash. Jerry Norton states that hard money, an asset lender or a private money investor still counts as cash in the industry, because the funds are liquid and not tied to a traditional full-approval process [R83ectOeUdU @ 00:01:09]. Brent Daniels explains why that capital is so accessible: private funds pay wealthy depositors roughly 6 to 10 percent, lend it back out at 12 or 14 percent, and earn most of their income on fees and points, so they are motivated to lend and want to be on the investor's team; the label 'hard' simply means they underwrite the property, not the borrower's credit, job history or reserves [AcL3tusr27o @ 00:03:38]. On a separate episode Daniels tells new wholesalers the same thing, fielding five to ten DMs a day asking how to get proof of funds and answering with one directive: find a financial partner or a hard money lender that will fund 100 percent on really good deals [HB5dJx0VOrA @ 00:00:46]. Foreclosure University backs the transactional version of that promise, offering to fund 100 percent of an A-to-B purchase including closing costs so the investor brings nothing out of pocket [38RXOgdabuQ @ 00:01:37].

At the closing table the consensus flips from proving money to protecting it. Katherine Brough tells buyers to verify every wire, not just last-minute changes, by calling the escrow officer on a number established early through an independent source, never by replying to the email or dialing a number printed inside it [h1TnczbK_bE @ 00:02:06]. PropLogix's title executive gives clients the identical rule, warning that someone is actively trying to steal their money and that they should only call from a number they have always had [k03c-6thJPg @ 00:00:42]. Kelsie Toole of Chicago Title explains why the stakes are absolute: once a bank wires money to the wrong party, it is gone and there is no getting it back [-9IO2PFhhdE @ 00:01:49]. The proration specialists apply the same verify-first discipline to the numbers themselves. Matthew Halliday's rule on Escrow Escapes is that cash to close is the answer, not the explanation, so buyers should make every line on the statement explain itself before signing, after a buyer caught an unexplained $800 special assessment at the table [kfe6mMfaivM @ 00:01:21]. Both camps agree that slowing down a closing costs minutes, while skipping verification can cost the deal, the down payment or the seller's net proceeds.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The letter-generation stack is cheap and fast. Brent Daniels runs three free routes: a local hard money lender's website where the investor types the property address and gets approved online for what the lender will advance on that asset, the proof of funds request form at doubleclose.com that emails the letter back, and besttransactionalfunding.com as the third option [AcL3tusr27o @ 00:07:15]. Steph Davis recommends Tailwind Funding, owned by a friend, at $1.99 per letter or $9.99 a month for unlimited letters; the investor enters the name exactly as it appears on the purchase contract, the property address and the purchase price, and the letter is emailed immediately, with no obligation to actually borrow from that lender [FOfp5iWKVkc @ 00:04:20]. Foreclosure University issues free letters through a funding request form but will not produce one without the buyer's individual or company name, the seller's name, the property address, the amount needed and contact information, and it demands every address even on bulk REO portfolios [rNJDrR6nTIk @ 00:00:16]. Jerry Norton's flipster software gives Pro and Prime members unlimited custom letters carrying the buyer's name, address and offer amount, generated by filling a couple of blanks and stored in a dashboard that emails them directly [R83ectOeUdU @ 00:11:20].

When an agent rejects the letter, the operators run scripted fallbacks. Flipping Mastery TV says roughly 90 percent of agents accept a soft letter as a box to check and about 10 percent want something hard; to that minority the operator offers a five-to-seven-day contingency, explaining that the investors who fund the deal will not look at it without an executed contract, so the agent can terminate if hard proof never arrives [9NXVYf_SZCA @ 00:04:07]. Jerry Norton's verbal script is to say the deal is being bought with hard money, hand over the soft letter, and promise a hard commitment letter once the property is under contract and approved; if the agent still balks, Norton's verdict is that the agent does not trust the buyer and the buyer needs a new agent [R83ectOeUdU @ 00:07:11]. Steph Davis used their father's line-of-credit statement for bank-owned offers and says it worked 99 percent of the time, with one or two agents questioning the name mismatch until told it was a money partner; Davis suggests paying a trusted friend or relative a couple hundred dollars or cutting them in on the deal [FOfp5iWKVkc @ 00:02:35]. If a bank still refuses a transactional letter, Davis rewrites the bid with a financing contingency and accepts a weaker offer [FUjDeT5p55I @ 00:02:13].

Closing-table math follows the same calendar logic every time. Matthew Halliday's worked example on Escrow Escapes: annual taxes estimated at $3,600 run roughly $10 a day, so a seller who owned the home 180 days of the tax period owes about $1,800, depending on what was already paid [kfe6mMfaivM @ 00:02:49]. Julee Felsman maps Oregon's version: the tax year runs July 1 to June 30, bills are due November 15, a closing from July 2 through November 14 earns the buyer a seller credit, a closing after November 15 means the buyer owes the seller, and lenders target 14 months of the prior year's taxes in escrow before the October bill [faIlHE0Vtco @ 00:08:14]. Felsman's shortcut is that prorations plus the escrow deposit total 11 to 12 months of taxes for most of the year, rising to 13 to 15 months during the September-to-early-October hold-and-pay window, when title collects about 115 percent of last year's bill, charges a $60 to $100 service fee and refunds the overage [faIlHE0Vtco @ 00:16:43]. House Math shows the stakes of skipping the bill on a paid-off property: penalties and interest can run more than 10 percent a year, and a county tax lien usually jumps ahead of even a mortgage [IDV1BO2CYmg @ 00:01:25].

callout.title: Small Details That Keep Letters Accepted and Closing Math Clean
callout.body: Execution details the practitioners use to stop agents, banks and closing statements from tripping up a funded deal.
items: Match the name on the proof to the name on the offer; agents tie bank statements to the buyer and will challenge a Jerry Norton statement attached to a John Doe offer [Flipping Mastery TV — 9NXVYf_SZCA @ 00:03:21].

Pull transactional lender letters without borrowing from them; enter the contract name, property address and loan amount online and the letter is emailed back [FlipThisWholesaler — FOfp5iWKVkc @ 00:03:50].
Confirm the closing agent or attorney knows the back-to-back process before funding; if not, replace them or have the funder walk them through it [Foreclosure University — 38RXOgdabuQ @ 00:02:40].

Ask the lender to itemize the generic seller credits line on the loan estimate, since a missing tax proration shifts the cash actually due at closing [Julee Felsman | Workshop Team | Guaranteed Rate — faIlHE0Vtco @ 00:05:39].

sop_steps.title: Lock a Local Funding Relationship
sop_steps.action: Search hard money lenders plus your city, enter the property address online, and keep a national letter source as backup.
sop_steps.detail: Local hard money letters give agents a warm and fuzzy feeling that out-of-state national brands do not; start local and fall back to doubleclose.com or besttransactionalfunding.com [Brent Daniels - Wholesaling Inc — AcL3tusr27o @ 00:05:51].

sop_steps.title: Attach a Matching Soft Letter to Every Cash Offer
sop_steps.action: Generate a custom letter carrying the buyer name, property address and offer amount for each offer submitted.
sop_steps.detail: Custom soft letters can be produced for as many deals as needed and state a lending relationship without committing funding to the specific deal [Flipping Mastery TV — R83ectOeUdU @ 00:05:37].

sop_steps.title: Script the Hard-Proof Objection
sop_steps.action: Offer a five-to-seven-day proof of funds contingency and explain funders need an executed contract first.
sop_steps.detail: Tell the agent the funding investors will not review the deal without a signed contract, so the seller can terminate if hard proof does not arrive in the window [Flipping Mastery TV — 9NXVYf_SZCA @ 00:04:07].

sop_steps.title: Verify Wires and Statement Lines Before Money Moves
sop_steps.action: Call escrow on the pre-verified number to confirm recipient, bank, routing, account and amount, then audit every unexplained line.
sop_steps.detail: Confirm the recipient name, bank, routing number, account number and amount on a trusted call [Katherine Brough — h1TnczbK_bE @ 00:02:20], and ask who is responsible, what period it covers and what document supports each highlighted line [Escrow Escapes — kfe6mMfaivM @ 00:08:59].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is where the letter comes from. Brent Daniels pushes local hard money first, arguing that a local lender letter beats a national brand because agents who dig into the background of an offer get a warm and fuzzy feeling from a local relationship, with doubleclose.com or besttransactionalfunding.com as free fallbacks when nothing local turns up [AcL3tusr27o @ 00:07:15]. Jerry Norton goes the opposite direction and sells volume: Pro and Prime members of Flipster get unlimited custom soft letters carrying the buyer name, property address and offer amount, generated instantly instead of waiting a couple of days on a lender who charges for them or rations them [R83ectOeUdU @ 00:05:09]. Steph Davis routes students to Tailwind Funding, where a letter runs a buck ninety-nine each or $9.99 a month for unlimited, and stresses that using the letter never obligates you to actually borrow from the lender issuing it [FOfp5iWKVkc @ 00:04:20]. Foreclosure University hands out free letters, but only against a real address, the buyer name, the seller name and the amount needed, and ties them directly to its transactional funding product [rNJDrR6nTIk @ 00:00:33]. The operator choice is speed and volume from a generator versus local credibility from a lender relationship that can actually fund the back half of the deal.

The bigger fight is what to do when an agent rejects the soft letter. Jerry Norton puts it at roughly 90% of agents accepting a soft letter to check a box and 10% wanting something hard, and for that 10% the playbook is negotiation: write a five, six or seven day contingency, because no investor funds without an executed contract, and terminate if hard proof never arrives [9NXVYf_SZCA @ 00:04:07]. In a separate breakdown, Norton is far blunter: the letter is fine, the agent simply does not believe you can close, and the move is to find a new agent [R83ectOeUdU @ 00:09:07]. Steph Davis takes a third route on bank-owned REOs: just make the offer and see what that bank accepts, and if it refuses a transactional letter, check the financing contingency box and let the bank treat it as a financed offer, weaker but still alive [FUjDeT5p55I @ 00:02:26]. On the Wholesaling Inc channel, Brent Daniels tells wholesalers to find a hard money lender that will give 100% on really good deals, and co-host Tom ties that backing to saying 'I am a cash buyer' with shoulders back and voice projected [HB5dJx0VOrA @ 00:02:01]. Pick the posture before the counteroffer lands, not after the listing agent pushes back.

On the wire side, the professionals disagree on how to move and verify the money. Kelsie Toole of Chicago Title accepts a cashier's check for closing funds under $100,000, requires a wire above that, calls to verify every cashier's check, and warns that the web is not always the best check because hackers build fake websites, preferring face-to-face or verbal verification [-9IO2PFhhdE @ 00:06:13]. Think Escrow points buyers to the number on the escrow website or on paper documents escrow sent, wants cashier's checks at least five days early, and has escrow leave the bank account number off emailed instructions so the recipient must call for it [f-7Rw_JAZOA @ 00:06:57]. PropLogix deliberately removed the realtor from handling wiring documents years ago, pushing buyers and sellers to contact the title company directly through an encrypted channel [k03c-6thJPg @ 00:03:34]. Sunny Fedorenko runs the opposite model, putting the realtor in the middle as protector: secure portals only, never email attachments, triple verification before funds move, a step-by-step walkthrough, and no last-minute changes without a phone call from multiple parties [j0SpK9C7lHs @ 00:04:33]. The common thread is an independently known phone number; the open split is whether the agent is the shield or the weakest link in the chain.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The proof-of-funds failures are predictable and they cluster around names and banks. Jerry Norton reports that agents are not stupid: hand over a bank statement showing Jerry Norton when the offer says John Doe, and the agent asks how the two are related and why you are handing over some random proof of funds [9NXVYf_SZCA @ 00:03:34]. Steph Davis lived that exact mismatch early on, using a statement from a father's line of credit on bank-owned offers; it worked 99% of the time, and the one or two challenges were settled by explaining the lender was a money partner [FOfp5iWKVkc @ 00:02:51]. The heavier trap is REO inventory, where Davis says acceptance depends on the bank, and some will refuse a transactional funding letter on a cash offer and demand an actual bank statement or a line of credit that is ready to go [FUjDeT5p55I @ 00:01:08]. The back end fails too: Foreclosure University warns that the investor must stay independent because the end buyer's money cannot fund the A-to-B leg, and that a closing agent or attorney who does not know the backtack process has to be replaced or shown exactly what to do [38RXOgdabuQ @ 00:02:23]. Every one of these surfaces after the seller signs, which is the most expensive moment to discover them.

Wire fraud losses are the hardest numbers on the table. Sunny Fedorenko cites a Southern California couple who lost $160,000 and an Orlando couple who lost $38,000 in escrow scams, and says that once a wire is gone the bank, the title company and the agent are not responsible [j0SpK9C7lHs @ 00:02:21]. Think Escrow describes a buyer in a multiple-offer bidding war who got a fake escrow email demanding an immediate good-faith deposit to lock in the purchase, rushed to the bank, drove home happy, and in a matter of half an hour the funds were already diverted into out-of-state accounts [f-7Rw_JAZOA @ 00:10:18]. The same escrow veteran recounts an escrow company that skipped looking at its outgoing wires for several days while fraudsters inside its accounting system generated wires in $10,000 and $20,000 increments totaling about $250,000 [f-7Rw_JAZOA @ 00:07:41]. PropLogix's title expert was spoofed supposedly ordering an office to wire a large sum, a request built from one internet search of name, email address and company [k03c-6thJPg @ 00:01:46]. Fedorenko adds that hackers now use AI mimicry: cloned signatures, hijacked threads, fake PDFs carrying escrow logos, and URLs identical except for one letter. Every loss above started with a message that looked legitimate.

The closing math hides its own traps, and they hit cash to close directly. Matthew Halliday of Escrow Escapes tells of a buyer holding the pen who found an extra $800 that turned out to be a special assessment, not routine HOA dues, and rejects the 'just sign and sort it out later' instinct because an unclear amount does not get clearer once the keys are in your hand [kfe6mMfaivM @ 00:04:43]. Julee Felsman flags that Oregon loan estimates frequently omit the property tax proration a buyer owes the seller, so the buyer must plan more cash than the lender estimated, and that a title company hold and pay typically collects about 115% of the prior year's bill plus a $60 to $100 tax payment service fee [faIlHE0Vtco @ 00:11:22]. Felsman adds a twist for anyone who negotiates hard: if the seller pays 100% of closing costs, the hold-and-pay refund check goes to the seller, not the buyer [faIlHE0Vtco @ 00:12:06]. House Math shows the downstream risk once escrow disappears: penalties and interest that can exceed 10% a year, and a county tax lien that jumps ahead of almost every other claim including a mortgage, followed by lien or house sales to investors [IDV1BO2CYmg @ 00:01:25].

callout.title: No Money Moves Until These Four Checks Clear
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a loss, a near-miss, or a surprise line item practitioners hit firsthand. Clear all four before funds leave the account or a pen touches the closing statement.
items: Verify every wire, not just changed ones, by calling escrow on a number established early and independently; never reply to the email or use a phone number printed in the message being verified [Katherine Brough — h1TnczbK_bE @ 00:02:06].
Treat any request to wire to a new bank account as a red flag, because title companies rarely change banking relationships and their information never changes [PropLogix — k03c-6thJPg @ 00:03:52].

If a wire looks compromised, call the bank immediately to recall it, notify escrow and the agent, and report to FBI IC3; international wires over 50,000 need a SWIFT recall within 72 hours [Think Escrow! — f-7Rw_JAZOA @ 00:08:49].
Highlight every closing statement line that cannot be explained in one sentence and get who, what period, and what document before signing [Escrow Escapes — kfe6mMfaivM @ 00:08:59].

chapters.pull_quote: "Cash to close is the answer, not the explanation. Before you sign, make the statement explain itself." — Escrow Escapes (kfe6mMfaivM @ 00:01:21).
action_checklist: Search hard money lenders plus your city, pick one or two local lenders, and enter the property address to get approved online for a proof of funds letter [Brent Daniels - Wholesaling Inc — AcL3tusr27o @ 00:06:10].

For transactional lender letters, enter the exact name on the purchase contract, the property address and the purchase price; Tailwind runs $1.99 per letter or $9.99 a month unlimited [FlipThisWholesaler — FOfp5iWKVkc @ 00:04:20].
When an agent demands hard proof, propose a five-to-seven-day contingency to deliver it after execution, with termination if it never arrives [Flipping Mastery TV — 9NXVYf_SZCA @ 00:04:07].
Early in escrow, ask the escrow officer how wiring instructions will arrive and how to verify them, then save a trusted phone number [Katherine Brough — h1TnczbK_bE @ 00:01:23].
Confirm the account number out loud over the phone before wiring; if one number is off, do not send the wire [Sunny Fedorenko — j0SpK9C7lHs @ 00:03:51].

Plan for 11 to 12 months of property taxes at an Oregon closing, and 13 to 15 months inside the September to early October hold-and-pay window [Julee Felsman | Workshop Team | Guaranteed Rate — faIlHE0Vtco @ 00:16:43].

chapters.question_prompt: What is the Gator Method, and how do people make money funding EMDs and other people's deals with little capital?
chapters.title: The Gator Method
chapters.subtitle: Gator lending vs. transactional lending, EMD funding and lender criteria, contracts for earnest money deposits, the seven Gator strategies, live-call deals and 200% returns, practitioner case studies, starting with little money, and critical reviews of the course and upsell concerns
chapters.executive_summary: Gator lending, as Pace Morby teaches it, means funding the small, fast checks big lenders ignore, wholesaler earnest money deposits first, and charging a flat chunk instead of interest. The consensus economics: $1,000 to $3,000 out, $1,500 to $3,000 back, with headline deals such as $1,500 returning $5,000 and $5,000 returning $3,000 in ten days. Safety rests on getting onto the HUD, a contract clause routing the deposit back to the lender, signed seller releases and title confirmation by email and phone. Abdiel Garcia Rodriguez publishes hard terms: 5% or $350 upfront, EMD loans up to 60 days, transactional money at 2% plus 0.2% per day. Crushing REI counters that EMD is overrated and posted about 10% of the time in Michigan, while Tom McKay's guest spent close to $10,000 across the stack and saw EMD offers draw no engagement.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus - Gators Eat the Dead Carcass Big Lenders Ignore
paragraphs: Every Pace Morby session lands on the same definition: a gator is a transactional lender who prices money in chunks rather than annual interest and runs a high count of fast in-and-out deals [x24Yz464jLE @ 00:01:27]. The contrast is the whale who parks capital at 7-10% just to preserve it. Pace argues ten percent a year on a $1,500 earnest money check is not worth a big lender's time, which leaves small EMD deals as the dead carcass that gators eat. He runs the math on stage: ten percent on $5,000 is only $500 a year, while his probate deal pays $10,000 on that same $5,000, a 200% hit [7yVZPbb03bc @ 00:13:41]. The street version is a $1,500 EMD advance that returns $5,000 at close while the wholesaler banks $25,000, with one non-negotiable condition: 'as long as I'm on the HUD' [-9RSC5hpr9o @ 00:04:29]. Even Crushing REI, which openly questions how much money the model makes, defines it the same way: lend wholesalers their EMD and get repaid at close 'plus 12 15 20%,' possibly higher, with the speaker unsure what rate the course recommends [jDAbeOWsBX4 @ 00:00:54]. The chunk, not the rate, is the product everyone agrees on.

Demand is the second point of agreement. Pace says 85% of wholesalers lack the cash for earnest money, and his average gator check runs $1,000 to $3,000 with $1,500 to $3,000 coming back [iVg9EsSij2c @ 00:00:46]. The squeeze comes from listing agents, who will not let an investor get under contract without EMD; on a $200,000 house they want 1-3%, meaning $2,000 down today and $198,000 at close on a 30-day contract, and wholesalers juggling five, six, or ten contracts run dry [qbBAO0ozP-0 @ 00:00:59]. Market averages climb fast: Pace pegs Phoenix at $5,000, Nevada at $4,000 and LA at $15,000 [aIHVhFGaNAw @ 00:04:20]. Crushing REI confirms the borrower profile from the other side, noting that large wholesalers likely already hold $1,000, so the realistic targets are broke newbies [jDAbeOWsBX4 @ 00:05:16]. Pace frames the imbalance as millions of wholesalers against a few thousand gators, and tells people sitting on cash that the market is literally paying for access: 'people are paying 25 Grand to find your 25 Grand.' The consensus prerequisite is not a big bankroll; Pace puts the cash needed to start lending at roughly $1,000 to $1,500, with a no-money path through credit lines and wrestling other gators.

The third consensus point is that the deposit only stays safe if title knows who owns it. Pace's contract carries an irrevocable instruction in Section seven returning the deposit 'to the buyer or any person or entity designated by the buyer' during inspection, and he warns that once the agent submits commission instructions, title must already know the EMD is lent and expects a return [qbBAO0ozP-0 @ 00:07:40]. His best-practice script is to email title confirming the due-diligence end date, the seller release, and that the EMD returns to the lender rather than the buyer or assignor, then follow up by phone [T5jtdYhM6tQ @ 00:07:01]. Abdiel Garcia Rodriguez builds the same guardrails into a written criteria sheet: funding only inside the inspection period with at least 48 hours left, a written understanding from title or escrow, and the fee paid directly to the gator [min0RpX32uc @ 00:05:30]. Even the critic lines up here; Crushing REI calls EMD lending an unsecured loan and says the mitigation is seeing the contract, knowing exactly when due diligence makes the deposit non-refundable, and keeping communication tight [jDAbeOWsBX4 @ 00:04:02]. Pace and Abdiel both run proper lending paperwork and a JV agreement, with a title officer in the loop, as the baseline before a single dollar moves.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The core Gator 1.0 waterfall is laid out with a $200,000 contract carrying a $2,000 EMD, a 30-day close and a 10-day inspection period [aIHVhFGaNAw @ 00:02:34]. The wholesaler assigns at $225,000 for a $25,000 fee; at closing the seller takes $198,000, the gator gets the $2,000 reimbursed plus a $5,000 chunk, and the wholesaler walks with $20,000 [aIHVhFGaNAw @ 00:10:00]. Pricing on a live call is relationship-based: repeat clients pay a flat fee around $2,000, first-timers pay roughly 30% of the wholesale fee. Justin, who stays under $500,000 purchase prices at 1% EMD so the deposit never tops $5,000, agreed to $3,000 flat going forward, while on the first deal Pace put in $2,000 and took $4,000 on top [A3l3Dg0cJLk @ 00:02:01]. Abdiel Garcia Rodriguez prices more formally: EMD loans capped at 60 days, a non-refundable upfront deposit of 5% or $350 minimum credited toward the fee, a fee calculated on calendar days, and typical fees of $3,000 to $4,000 on deposits in the $3,000 to $10,000 range, rarely over $15,000, with capacity up to $100,000 [min0RpX32uc @ 00:04:24]. On the house split Pace reported, a $20,000 profit left the house $6,500 and the gator $13,500.

Beyond EMD, the ladder moves into transactional money. Pace pegs the average double close at $400,000 priced at 1-3 points, or $4,000 to $12,000 for a single day [iVg9EsSij2c @ 00:02:40]. Abdiel Garcia Rodriguez prices transactional funding at 2% for the first 24 hours with a $2,000 minimum plus 0.2% per day, always funded to escrow, capped at seven days and wired in under 48 hours across all 50 states [min0RpX32uc @ 00:07:09]. Gator 2.0 as Pace teaches it on one stage is a referral play: send borrowers to myinvestorloan.com for 1 point, for example $2,250 on a $225,000 loan, with zero risk and a lifetime point on repeat loans; he says he referred $75 million last year and was paid $750,000 [aIHVhFGaNAw @ 00:15:20]. The advanced version raises money at 10% and lends at 16-18% plus 2 points, but only after an operator hits $15,000 to $30,000 a month and 15 to 30 deals. The bigger tickets come through escrow: Luis needed $300,000 parked in escrow as proof for a conventional refinance, the cash sat two days without moving, and the deal paid 2 points, 1 to the capital partner and 1 split between Dan and Aaron Kim [z2rCv8gn1cE @ 00:07:07].

Sourcing is a phone game. Pace's line is 'call a title company,' backed by Facebook wholesaler groups, YouTube comments and double closes, plus a three-part pitch that offers to underwrite deals, revive dead leads and provide transactional lending [7yVZPbb03bc @ 00:35:09]. Dan's version targets investor-friendly title shops after generic ones rejected the pitch; from a 250-name list roughly every tenth officer said they 'could have used you last week,' and one later emailed asking for $400,000 for two days [z2rCv8gn1cE @ 00:24:54]. Pace backs those relationships with about $5,000 a year in escrow-officer gifts such as Nordstrom cards and flowers, and claims one escrow officer can feed 50 lifetime deals. Capital for the chunks comes from credit: a student with poor credit got a $2,000 line in two weeks through Prime Corporate Services, and Pace funded his Justin deal off a PCS line, calling it a '200 return' in nine days [A3l3Dg0cJLk @ 00:04:58]. The tool stack splits by tier, with paceandabraham.com handling EMD and Alpha Gator handling double closes, DSCR, hard money and commercial loans, which Pace calls 'the shovel' rather than the training [_WfyIRKBE8o @ 00:01:29]. No-cash operators are told to JV, 'Gator wrestle' other lenders, and comment 'I have money to lend here's my Ig' on raise-capital YouTube videos.

callout.title: Lock the Release Before You Wire
callout.body: The money is made at contracting and at title, not at closing. These are the moves practitioners use to make sure the deposit comes back to the gator.
items: Have the seller pre-sign the title company's EMD release form at contracting and leave it in the file with a sticky note, because title policy can demand signed authorization even when the contract already allows the return [Pace Morby — qbBAO0ozP-0 @ 00:14:54].
In mutual release states such as Texas and Utah the seller must consent to release EMD, so Pace's contract has the seller waive that consent up front [Pace Morby — A3l3Dg0cJLk @ 00:03:40].
Before lending, ask the borrower how many deals they have completed; 25 completed deals is the signal Pace flags as worth funding [Pace Morby — OBl7C-hFLY4 @ 00:07:13].

Write a daily late fee into longer loans by taking the monthly fee, dividing by 30 and pushing it up a little; Pace's $65,000 first-position loan carried $500 a day [Pace Morby — S9WonQBbHG8 @ 00:43:59].

sop_steps.title: Source Wholesalers Through Title and Escrow
sop_steps.action: Call investor-friendly title companies and pitch underwriting, dead-lead revival and transactional lending.
sop_steps.detail: Skip generic title shops and work an investor-friendly list; roughly every tenth officer on a 250-name list said they could have used a gator last week [Pace Morby — z2rCv8gn1cE @ 00:22:36]. Back it with a transactional-funding website carrying a selfie video and Calendly link [Pace Morby — 7yVZPbb03bc @ 00:38:09].

sop_steps.title: Screen and Price the Request
sop_steps.action: Confirm the inspection window, collect an upfront fee and set a flat or percentage chunk.
sop_steps.detail: Fund only inside the inspection period with at least 48 hours remaining and take 5% or $350 minimum upfront, credited toward the fee [Abdiel Garcia Rodriguez — min0RpX32uc @ 00:05:30]. Pace charges $200 to $1,000 upfront to filter bad deals [Pace Morby — T5jtdYhM6tQ @ 00:05:26].

sop_steps.title: Paper the Deal and Route the Deposit
sop_steps.action: Execute the JV and EMD loan documents and instruct title where the EMD returns.
sop_steps.detail: Use a JV agreement, EMD loan agreement, assignment of EMD and signed mutual release [Abdiel Garcia Rodriguez — min0RpX32uc @ 00:02:59]. Pace's TC tells the attorney where the EMD returns under attorney-drafted gator docs [Pace Morby — A3l3Dg0cJLk @ 00:02:30].

sop_steps.title: Confirm With Title, Wire, Collect on the HUD
sop_steps.action: Email and call title, wire to escrow, and collect reimbursement plus the chunk at close.
sop_steps.detail: Email title confirming due-diligence end date, seller release and lender routing, then follow up by phone [Pace Morby — T5jtdYhM6tQ @ 00:07:01]. Release funds only once the gator is on the HUD [Pace Morby — 7yVZPbb03bc @ 00:12:40].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fault line is whether earnest money is even the choke point. Pace Morby builds the entire Gator 1.0 thesis on it: agents will not let an investor get under contract without EMD, and on a $200,000 house that means $2,000 to $6,000 in cash on day one [qbBAO0ozP-0 @ 00:01:33]. Pace puts the share of wholesalers without EMD at 85%, with a typical outlay of $1,000 to $3,000 returning $1,500 to $3,000 [iVg9EsSij2c @ 00:00:46]. Crushing REI pushes back hard from a Michigan shop closing over 100 deals a year: they post earnest money maybe 10% of the time and never lead with it, because most sellers do not ask for EMD unless a realtor represents them [jDAbeOWsBX4 @ 00:02:35]. Their read is that EMD is overrated, an inspection contingency makes it almost always refundable, and a Gator has to hunt down wholesalers who consistently post deposits, which may be more common in other states or bigger cities. Abdiel Garcia Rodriguez splits the difference by widening the lane beyond wholesale EMD into fix-and-flip deposits, double closes and seller carryback, so a Gator is not dependent on one deal type to stay deployed [min0RpX32uc @ 00:02:38]. The operator takeaway is market-specific: test local contract habits before assuming EMD demand exists.

Pricing is the second split, and nobody quotes the same rate card. Pace Morby charges a chunk rather than interest: a flat fee around $2,000 for repeat clients and roughly 30% of the wholesale fee for first-timers, which on Justin's deal became $3,000 flat going forward and $4,000 on top of a $2,000 deposit for the first close [A3l3Dg0cJLk @ 00:01:05]. Abdiel Garcia Rodriguez runs a calendar-day model instead, collecting an upfront deposit of 5% or a $350 minimum that is non-refundable but credited toward the fee, with the fee paid at close of escrow from the assignment fee or a private money lender [min0RpX32uc @ 00:02:59]. On transactional money, Abdiel prices 2% for the first 24 hours with a $2,000 minimum, plus 0.2% per day, always funded to escrow, on terms capped at seven days [min0RpX32uc @ 00:07:09]. Crushing REI describes the play as repayment at close plus 12, 15 or 20%, and admits being unsure what rate Pace actually recommends [jDAbeOWsBX4 @ 00:00:54]. Whichever card you run, decide before the first call whether you sell a percentage, a flat chunk, or a daily meter. The spread between these models is wide enough that two Gators funding the identical $2,000 deposit can walk away with very different checks.

The third split is whose money goes into the deal and what it costs to get in the door. Pace Morby calls lending your own cash being lazy, and offers to fund a new Gator's first 10 transactions on a 70/30 split with 70% to the Gator [aIHVhFGaNAw @ 00:17:59]. When students complained that building credit takes too long, Pace told them to JV and Gator wrestle with capital holders instead, pointing at $180,000, $250,000 and $500,000 offers dropped into a single live chat [OBl7C-hFLY4 @ 00:01:44]. Tom McKay counters from the other side of the ledger: money is cheapest directly from a bank and private money lending is expensive, and the guest Mike, a Massachusetts police officer, stacked close to $10,000 across the sub-to course, the Gator program with lead-gen, two LLCs, tax help and corporate-credit coaching [cvQX0jcvIFc @ 00:17:05]. Pace's pricing ladder has the Gator price climbing to $5,900 with 3.0 and $7,900 with 4.0, with existing members paying nothing extra [_WfyIRKBE8o @ 00:03:22]. Tom's filter is blunt: do not buy anything that is not worth considerably more than you pay, and check Reddit and the BBB first. Mike also reports that the community is flooded with private-money requests driven by connector fees, which cuts against the idea that capital is the easy part.
